text:
Qwen3.8-35B-A3B just got tested in a real agentic coding benchmark, and the result is pretty revealing.

I ran Empero’s Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill through my own benchmark using the Pi Agent harness.

20 real multi-step bug-fix tasks.

Same hardware for everything:

RTX 3060 12GB
16GB system RAM

The goal wasn’t to force every model into the same quantization.

It was simpler:

What is the strongest model you can actually run on this kind of hardware and use as an agent?

The results:

Qwen3.8-27B IQ2_XS: 16/20
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: 16/20
Ornith-1.5-35B: 15/20
Ornith-1.5-9B: 12/20
Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill: 10/20

The surprising part is that Qwen3.8-27B at 2-bit still matched the best score and beat every 4-bit model in this run.

The Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill was the bigger surprise.

It finished 6 tasks behind Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the architecture it was distilled into.

But the raw 10/20 score doesn’t tell the whole story.

9 of its 10 failures were caused by runaway thinking.

6 tasks hit the output cap.

Another 3 had to be killed because the model kept looping instead of progressing toward the fix.

When it actually started editing the code, the picture changed completely.

It solved 10 of 11 tasks where it got to the editing stage.

That suggests the main problem in this checkpoint isn’t necessarily the coding ability itself. The agent loop and reasoning behavior are getting in the way.

And that’s exactly why I care more about agentic benchmarks than a single static coding score.

A model can look great on a benchmark where it gets one prompt and unlimited time to answer.

Put it inside an agent.

Give it a repository.

Make it inspect files, modify code, run tests, recover from failures and manage its own context.

Now you find out what actually survives.

Empero says training is still continuing from this checkpoint, so I’m not treating this as the final verdict.

Once the final Qwen3.8-35B-A3B distill weights are released, I’ll run the same 20 tasks again.

Same hardware. Same harness. Same benchmark.

Then we’ll see how much the extra training changes the agentic result.

text:
𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐇𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩𝐬 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠?

I’ve been thinking about this one lately.

We talk a lot about making AI smarter.

Better models.
Better reasoning.
Better Agents.
Better Skills.

But there’s another problem that doesn’t get talked about enough:

Memory.

Because imagine having a really capable AI Agent that can solve complex problems…

…but every Skill keeps its own little island of information.

One Skill knows about the project.
Another knows about the tasks.
Another has different context.
And the Agent has to piece everything together again.

That gets messy pretty fast.

What if AI could actually maintain structured memory that different Skills could share?

That’s where things get interesting.

Instead of memory being just a giant text blob, imagine information being stored as structured objects:

𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧 → 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 → 𝐓𝐚𝐬𝐤 → 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭 → 𝐃𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭

with relationships connecting them.

So an Agent doesn’t just remember something.

It can understand what that information is, how it relates to other information, and what depends on what.

And this is where one Finch Skill I found really caught my attention.

The ontology Skill on Finch is designed as a typed knowledge graph for structured Agent memory and composable Skills. It lets entities have types, properties, and relationships, while mutations are checked against constraints before being committed. 

That sounds technical, but the idea is actually pretty simple.

Imagine I tell an Agent:

“Remember that Project X is connected to Task Y.”

Later, another Skill can access that same information.

Then another Skill can update it.

No need for every Skill to maintain a completely separate private memory.

Shared state → Shared context → Composable Skills

That could make multi-step AI workflows way more interesting.

For example:

Agent researches a project

Important information gets stored

Another Skill reads that information

A Task gets connected to the project

The Agent continues from the existing context

Instead of:

Okay, what did we know about this again?

The Agent can build on what it already knows.

And there’s another cool part.

The same structured graph can represent dependencies and even multi step plans, so questions like What depends on this? can be handled through relationships in the graph rather than simply guessing from text. 

That changes how I think about AI memory.

It’s not just about remembering more.

It’s about remembering information in a way that other AI capabilities can actually understand and use.

And that fits nicely with the bigger direction I see in @FinchTechCN .ai.

Finch is building around Agents, Skills, Tasks, and an AI native marketplace where capabilities can connect with real work. 

But if Agents are going to handle longer and more complicated workflows, they need more than intelligence.

They need context that survives from one step to the next.

Because the real power might not come from an AI that remembers everything.

It could come from an AI ecosystem where different Skills can share the right information, update it, and build on each other’s work.

So maybe the next big question isn’t:

How smart can AI become?

Maybe it’s:

How much useful context can AI carry forward?

Because once AI stops forgetting…

every new Task doesn’t have to start from zero.

➜ Protocol statistics
➜ Smart Allocator information
➜ Public analytics across supported chains

No wallet is required for these public analytics.

5️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀

The analytics layer does not sign transactions.

It does not hold private keys.

It does not have permission to execute protocol writes.

This creates a clear separation between:

➜ Looking at information
➜ Taking an action

The analytics layer informs the agent.

The official MCP handles supported actions.

6️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗼𝗹 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

The official USDD MCP provides access to wallet and network state, protocol reads, and supported write operations.

This includes workflows involving:

➜ Vaults
➜ PSM
➜ Savings
➜ Token transfers
➜ Treasury information
➜ Smart Allocator

This is where wallet context and live protocol state become important.

7️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗥𝘂𝗹𝗲

Think of it this way.

You want to know the current USDD APY.

➜ Use analytics.

You want to check your wallet balance.

➜ Use the official MCP.

You want to inspect a Vault.

➜ Use the official MCP.

You want to perform a PSM swap.

➜ Use the official MCP through the skill workflow.

Different job, different tool.

8️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗖𝗟𝗜

USDD Skills also provides command line access to the analytics layer.

This means developers can retrieve the same public analytics from a terminal or automated development environment.

The output can be structured as JSON.

That makes it useful for developers who want to work with USDD data without needing an AI agent for every request.

9️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗻 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗗𝗼?

Imagine asking:

“Compare USDD Earn APY across supported networks.”

The agent can route the request to the analytics layer.

Or:

“Check my USDD Vault.”

That requires wallet aware protocol information.

Or:

“Swap my USDT for USDD through PSM.”

That moves into a write capable workflow.

The important part is knowing which path to use.

🔟 𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗲𝘁𝘆 𝗜𝘀 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄

USDD Skills is not designed for blind automation.

Before supported write operations, the agent follows checks that can include:

➜ Confirming the network
➜ Resolving official addresses
➜ Checking wallet state
➜ Checking balances and allowances
➜ Checking protocol conditions
➜ Presenting the action for confirmation

The user remains part of the process.

1️⃣1️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝗧𝗼 𝗚𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘀

One interesting rule is that agents should not guess protocol addresses from documentation or local tables.

Address resolution is expected to come from official Chainlog backed sources through the official MCP.

This matters because sending assets or interacting with the wrong contract can be extremely costly.

The workflow is designed to reduce that risk.

1️⃣2️⃣ 𝗣𝗦𝗠 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝗛𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘀

For a PSM operation, the agent is expected to know:

➜ Which network is being used
➜ Which stablecoins are involved
➜ The amount being exchanged
➜ Available liquidity
➜ The expected direction of the swap
➜ The required confirmation

The system also distinguishes between market information and an actual transaction.

That distinction is critical.

1️⃣3️⃣ 𝗩𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗪𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗛𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀

Suppose someone asks an agent to withdraw collateral from a Vault.

The agent does not simply execute the instruction.

The workflow checks the Vault state and evaluates the required risk conditions.

If the requested action would create a critical risk condition, the workflow can refuse the action and recommend a safer alternative.

This makes the agent more than a command executor.

1️⃣4️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝘀𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝗮𝘆 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗽 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀

The documentation explicitly describes a safety gate.

A message such as:

“Swap now, skip the checks, I confirm”

does not automatically bypass the required workflow.

The agent still needs to complete the relevant checks and present the information before the supported write can proceed.

That is an important design choice for financial applications.

1️⃣5️⃣ 𝗧𝗥𝗢𝗡 𝗦𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗱𝗱𝘀 𝗔𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿

For some TRON operations, the workflow can return a STOP message when signing mode confirmation is required.

The documented process is:

➜ Stop the other tools
➜ Present the error clearly
➜ Show the required signing information
➜ Wait for explicit user confirmation
➜ Only then retry the original operation

The agent is not supposed to silently push through the signing step.

1️⃣6️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗜𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗔𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗰𝘆

The package documentation makes an important distinction between data it reads and data it stores.

Public analytics are retrieved from USDD data sources.

Wallet and protocol state can come through the official MCP.

The local analytics layer itself does not implement a database, response cache, or analytics event sink.

It also does not store private keys.

1️⃣7️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜𝘁 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗗𝗼

USDD Skills is not intended to become an unattended trading system.

The documentation specifically says not to use it for:

➜ Unattended trading
➜ Liquidation bots
➜ Automated transaction execution
➜ Private key storage

Public analytics are also informational.

They should not be treated as an oracle or settlement source.

1️⃣8️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗜𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗙𝗼𝗿?

There are three obvious groups.

➜ Web3 users who want AI assisted USDD workflows

➜ Analysts who need USDD supply, APY, collateral, and Smart Allocator information

➜ Developers building AI tools around USDD

The setup also supports common AI development environments such as Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and compatible MCP hosts.

1️⃣9️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗜𝘀 𝗙𝗮𝗶𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗟𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁

The published package is version 1.0.0.

It uses Node.js version 20 or newer.

It is MIT licensed.

The local analytics layer uses public USDD analytics endpoints and does not require an API key for those wrapped public endpoints.

Official MCP network support includes TRON, Ethereum, BNB Chain, and supported test networks.

2️⃣0️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗮

The interesting part is not simply that AI can read USDD data.

The bigger idea is giving an AI agent a structured operating layer.

It can understand what information is public.

It can distinguish wallet aware information from public analytics.

It can route supported actions through the official protocol interface.

And it can follow predefined safety checks before writes.

2️⃣1️⃣ 𝗜𝗻 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀

Think of USDD Skills as a set of instructions and tools that helps an AI agent understand:

“What can I read?”

“What can I check?”

“What requires a wallet?”

“What requires user confirmation?”

“What should never be guessed?”

“What should never be automated blindly?”

That structure is what makes the concept interesting.

2️⃣2️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝗦𝗗𝗗 𝗔𝗜 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄

A simplified flow looks like this:

➜ Ask the agent

➜ Identify the type of request

➜ Choose the appropriate MCP tool

➜ Retrieve the required data

➜ Run the relevant checks

➜ Present the action and its details

➜ Get user confirmation when required

➜ Execute through the official workflow

It creates a much clearer boundary between information and action.

2️⃣3️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀

DeFi can already be difficult for experienced users.

There are networks to select.

Contracts to verify.

Balances to check.

Allowances to understand.

Protocol conditions to inspect.

Transactions to review.

Now imagine having an AI agent that can help navigate those steps while following a predefined workflow instead of improvising every action.

That is where USDD Skills becomes interesting.

2️⃣4️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆

USDD Skills is building a bridge between AI agents and the USDD protocol.

Not just a chatbot that talks about DeFi.

A structured system that can:

➜ Read public USDD analytics

➜ Understand wallet aware protocol state

➜ Work with Vault, PSM, and Earn workflows

➜ Access USDD data through CLI tools

➜ Route supported writes through the official MCP

➜ Apply safety checks before sensitive actions

AI is moving closer to interacting with financial protocols.

The real question is how safely and transparently those interactions are designed.

USDD Skills offers one approach to that problem.

text:
$ZETA : Review 📜

What if a blockchain looked at its own numbers, decided it did not need to be a blockchain anymore, and asked its holders to vote it out of existence?

Meet ZetaChain, the universal Layer 1 that raised $27 million to connect every chain, and whose holders just voted 99.4% to shut it down and move to Solana.

What survives is ZETA itself, reborn as a Solana token, and Anuma, a private AI app the team now considers the actual product.

Let's explore one of the rarest decisions in crypto: a chain choosing to end.
👇

Marketplace Insight: ZetaChain's original pitch, a universal blockchain letting apps reach Bitcoin, Ethereum, and every other chain natively, landed in the most crowded and winner-takes-all corner of crypto, where interoperability protocols compete on network effects and second place is barely distinguishable from tenth.

The L1 never pulled enough builders to justify running its own chain. The clean contrast is that most projects in that position keep the chain alive on inertia and emissions. ZetaChain's team told holders the truth, proposed shutting it down, and 99.4% agreed. That is a failure of the original thesis and an unusually honest response to it, both at the same time.

⚪ Mission

ZetaChain's mission has shifted from connecting blockchains to connecting AI models under user control. The argument behind Anuma is that people's conversation history, preferences, and context are currently locked inside whichever AI company they happen to use, and that this memory should belong to the user, encrypted and portable across models. The token's role narrows accordingly, from gas and security for a whole chain to access for a private AI product running on Solana's infrastructure.

🔵 A Brief History

ZetaChain launched with an ambitious interoperability thesis, raising $27 million in 2023 from investors including Blockchain com and Jane Street. Its mainnet connected Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB Chain through an omnichain EVM that could manage native assets on connected chains without wrapping, and early on it ranked among the top blockchains by active users with over 100 million transactions and thousands of deployed contracts.

Validators included stc Bahrain, and partnerships extended to Korean telecom Stage Five and Maeil Business Newspaper's Mblock.
The token told a different story. ZETA fell roughly 97% from its February 2024 high of $2.85, and monthly unlocks of around 44 million tokens kept adding supply.

The interoperability market consolidated around a handful of winners, and ZetaChain's own chain never drew the developer base its design required. In April 2026 a Gateway cross-chain exploit hit team wallets for roughly $318,000 to $334,000, with the team stating no user funds were lost, and the cross-chain deposit and messaging features at the heart of the original product were wound down afterward, with deposits closing around June. By summer the interoperability thesis was effectively already retired.

The pivot had begun in January 2026 with ZetaChain 2.0 and an AI Portal routing across multiple model providers. February brought Anuma, a private AI app built on an encrypted Private Memory Layer, which integrated a rapid run of frontier models through the spring, including GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Kimi K2.6, and Qwen 3.6 Max. It crossed 300,000 users in mid-September.

On 17 September the team opened a 72-hour vote to shut the L1 down and migrate ZETA to Solana, citing faster execution, lower costs, deeper consumer liquidity, and existing AI-agent infrastructure, along with the ongoing cost of coordinating every upstream Cosmos security patch across independent validators. The late-August Cosmos EVM module exploits, which hit six other chains but not ZetaChain, were named as an example of that burden. The vote closed on 20 September at 99.4% in favour.

A second proposal covering the snapshot height, shutdown block, claims process, exchange conversion window, and withdrawal of assets from connected chains will follow once exchanges confirm the swap mechanism.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organizing idea has changed completely: from a chain that connects everything to an AI product that runs on someone else's chain.

➛ Anuma and the Private Memory Layer. Users' conversation history and preferences are encrypted and user-owned, following them across 35 AI models rather than staying locked inside any single AI company, with over 1.2 million requests and 30 billion tokens routed through its Bifrost gateway.

➛ A wallet in every account. Every Anuma account is a wallet, so the migration brings 300,000-plus users onto Solana on day one, into an ecosystem with sub-second execution and existing agent payment rails like x402.

➛ Direct issuance rather than a bridge. ZETA becomes a native Solana SPL token through fresh issuance, because a wrapped token would still depend on an origin chain that is scheduled to stop existing.

➛ Verifiable migration. A published snapshot export and checksum, plus a maintained archive node and explorer, let any holder independently confirm their converted balance.

➛ The Helium precedent. Helium moved its L1 to Solana across 2022 and 2023 and is generally regarded as having done so successfully, giving ZetaChain a working template for holder continuity.

➛ Frontier model routing. The AI Portal integrates models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Moonshot, and Alibaba, so Anuma sits above the model layer rather than competing with it directly, with a real-life social discovery feature now in beta.

⚪ Token Utilities

$ZETA's role is contracting from chain asset to app access token.

➛ AI credits: users lock ZETA to access AI credits inside Anuma, the primary utility after migration.

➛ Governance: holders vote through ZetaHub, including the second proposal that will finalize the migration.

➛ Staking and gas: still active on the L1 until wind-down, then retired, since Solana validators will secure native ZETA.

➛ Note on scope: ZETA on Ethereum and BNB Chain is excluded from the conversion and stays under existing terms, and balances convert from 18 to 9 decimals, rounded down.

⚪ Key Features

➛ A private AI app with user-owned, encrypted memory portable across 35 models.

➛ A 1:1 migration to Solana with no new tokens and vesting preserved.

➛ Direct issuance avoiding bridge risk entirely.

➛ Public snapshot, checksum, and archive node for balance verification.

➛ Governance that passed a chain shutdown at 58% turnout.

🔵 Meet the Team

ZetaChain is led by a compact core team that designed the universal blockchain, then proposed shutting it down when it did not find its market, which is a rarer and harder call than most teams ever make.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Ankur Nandwani - Co-Founder | Co-founded ZetaChain and led it from the universal interoperability thesis through the 2023 raise to the decision to retire the L1 and rebuild around Anuma.

➛ Charlie Pyle - Co-Founder | Co-founded the project and has helped steer the strategic pivot from cross-chain infrastructure toward private AI, including the move to Solana.

➛ Charlie McCowan - Head of Cyber Security and DevOps | Owns security and infrastructure operations, a load-bearing role given the April gateway exploit, the ongoing cost of Cosmos patch coordination the team cited as a reason to leave, and a migration that has to move every balance without error.

➛ Jonathan Covey [ @DAOist_JC ] - Head of Community | Runs community and governance engagement, the function behind a 58% turnout on Proposal 68, exceptional participation by crypto standards.

➛ Denis Fadeev - Head of Developer Experience | Leads developer tooling and documentation, the work that will determine how smoothly builders follow ZETA and Anuma onto Solana.

➛ Backers and ZetaHub | The 2023 raise of $27 million included Blockchain com and Jane Street, and ZetaHub runs both migration votes, including the second proposal that will set the snapshot height and timeline.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★ (3/5). The original use case, universal cross-chain infrastructure, is being retired because it did not attract enough builders to sustain its own chain, and that has to be the starting point. What replaces it is genuinely interesting: Anuma's user-owned, encrypted memory that follows people across 35 AI models addresses a real problem, 300,000 reported users in seven months is fast early growth, and every account arriving on Solana as a wallet gives the token a ready-made user base. The 2-point deduction is that the new thesis is seven months old with self-reported metrics, it competes for attention against every AI interface in the market, and the token's function is narrowing from securing a chain to unlocking credits in one app.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★ (3/5). The migration itself is handled cleanly: 1:1 conversion, no new tokens, a 2.1 billion maximum supply held constant, vesting schedules preserved, and a direct lock-for-credits sink inside Anuma. The 2-point deduction is contraction and overhang. Once the L1 shuts down, ZETA loses its gas and staking roles entirely, leaving AI credit access as the core utility. Monthly unlocks of around 44 million tokens continue, balances round down on the move from 18 to 9 decimals, and ZETA on Ethereum and BNB Chain is left outside the conversion, fragmenting the holder base.

➛ Audits: ★★★ (3/5). The migration design is genuinely security-conscious. Direct issuance removes bridge risk rather than managing it, the published snapshot and checksum make every converted balance independently verifiable, and the team cited the cost of coordinating Cosmos security patches across independent validators as a reason to leave. The 2-point deduction is the record and the disclosure. In April 2026 a Gateway cross-chain exploit drained roughly $318,000 to $334,000 from team wallets, an exploit in the core component of an interoperability chain, after which those features were wound down. No user funds were reported lost, which matters, but a demonstrated exploit in the flagship component outweighs the rest. I could not verify a named audit or security score for the Solana token or Anuma, and the migration itself is a high-risk operation not yet executed.

➛ Community: ★★★⯪ (3.5/5). 58% turnout on a governance vote is exceptional in crypto, where single-digit participation is common, and 99.4% approval for shutting down the project's own chain shows a holder base willing to accept an honest assessment rather than cling to the original story. Anuma's reported 300,000 users give the community a live product to rally around. The 1.5-point deduction is that the week's rally is governance-driven speculation on a vote rather than a completed swap, much of the original ecosystem built for the L1 will not follow it to Solana, and holders on Ethereum and BNB Chain are left navigating a separate path.

🔵 Conclusion

ZetaChain did something almost no project in this industry does. It looked at an original thesis that had not worked, a universal blockchain that never pulled enough builders to justify itself, and asked holders to shut it down. They agreed at 99.4% on 58% turnout.

What survives is a token reborn on Solana and Anuma, a private AI app with a genuinely differentiated idea: your AI memory should belong to you and follow you across every model.
The risks are real. The flagship thesis failed, its cross-chain gateway was exploited in April, and the token lost roughly 97% of its value before the vote.

The replacement product is seven months old with self-reported numbers, and the token's utility shrinks from securing a chain to unlocking credits in one app. Unlocks continue, holders on Ethereum and BNB Chain sit outside the conversion, and the week's rally is speculation on a vote rather than a completed swap. The second proposal that actually executes the migration has not been scheduled.

But the bull case has a precedent. Helium made the same move to Solana and came out the other side with its network intact, and ZetaChain is executing its version with more care than most chains take over anything: direct issuance, published checksums, preserved vesting, and exchanges confirmed before a single token moves. ZetaChain spent three years trying to be the chain everything connects to.

It is now betting that owning your AI memory is the more valuable idea. The honesty of the pivot is not in question. Whether the pivot works is.

Your agent memory shouldn’t be a pile of embeddings.

BrainAPI is a knowledge-graph-powered AI memory layer for builders who need to turn documents, notes, messages, or events into queryable context.

It helps you retrieve grounded context for a plain-language question by having specialized agents extract entities, create event-centric relationships, and return graph paths alongside the result.

Key features:

• Event-centric graph – models who did what, to whom, when, and in what context as event hubs
• Context retrieval – returns graph triples, passages, historical context, and optional provenance for a query
• Traceable answers – the README’s example exposes the graph path used to derive an answer
• Two pipeline modes – choose the full validation-focused accurate mode or a lighter extraction path
• Multiple integration paths – run the REST API, MCP server, console, and worker through the provided CLI

The code is publicly available under the Business Source License 1.1: non-production use is free; production use requires a commercial license.

text:
TermiX Agent Skills

Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI can install a portable skill package that lets them register an identity, stake, take jobs, and settle payments directly through AACP. No custom integration work required, just installing the skill and the agent gains commerce capabilities.

REST APIs and smart contracts

For teams building custom agents, TermiX exposes REST APIs alongside the underlying smart contracts. This means developers can integrate at whatever level fits their stack, either calling high-level endpoints or interacting with the protocol directly on-chain.

Event streams

Real-time event streams let developers track job postings, bids, deliveries, and settlements as they happen, useful for building dashboards, automation, or agents that react to marketplace activity in real time.

MCP compatibility

Because TermiX integrates with the Model Context Protocol ecosystem, agents built on MCP-compatible frameworks can tap into AACP without needing a bespoke connector for every tool.

Why this matters

An agent economy only works if agents can actually join it without friction. By meeting developers where they already build, through familiar coding tools, standard APIs, and existing protocols like MCP, TermiX lowers the barrier between “agent that can complete tasks” and “agent that can earn from them.”

This is the layer that usually gets skipped in agent economy conversations, but it’s the one that determines whether adoption actually happens.

That contrast says more about my nine @termix_ai posts than any feature list could.

Machine customers.
Agents hiring more specialized agents.

Then I started putting real orders through the marketplace.

TermiX was showing 584 listings at the time.

Discovery was easy.

Useful read only work could begin before a wallet entered the flow at all.

Then came the $19.90 GoPlus security order.

The first delivery did not include the source level evidence I had explicitly asked for.

So I sent it back.

The revised report added function references, technical details, root cause, impact and remediation.

That met the acceptance criterion.

I accepted the delivery and released escrow.

Then I went to the opposite extreme.

One dollar.

A custom HoloCard arrived in roughly ten minutes with an interactive viewer, source layers and a high resolution render.

I tested the viewer myself.

Rotation, flip, foil intensity and depth controls all worked.

There was still friction.

On my Android setup, opening index.html directly from the extracted folder did not load the experience correctly.

brief
escrow
delivery
inspection
rework or refund when needed
acceptance
settlement

That is what changed my view of TermiX.

The agent matters.

But a marketplace also has to keep its structure when the provider never shows up, when the first delivery misses the brief, and when the job is worth only one dollar.

After nine posts and several real orders, that is the part of TermiX I understand much better now.

text:
We tested JEV in GrowthOS, Rippling’s agent harness for GTM, using anonymized real-world data.

E.g. a marketer or RevOps user could ask, “Classify these campaign emails by strategy,” then analyze which messaging patterns perform best.

JEV achieved 90% accuracy versus 50% for the LLM baseline and ran nearly 8x faster.

It was not a universal win. JEV performed poorly as a control mechanism inside our text-to-SQL agent loop because it lacked the  semantic context needed to interpret internal business definitions. 

JEV could see that a query returned rows, but not know whether those rows represented Rippling’s canonical definition of “qualified pipeline.” The LLM could inspect the relevant models, filters, and business definitions before deciding whether the analysis was complete.

The takeaway: JEV looks extremely promising for repeatable 'classification' like workloads, while LLMs remain better suited to context-heavy reasoning. But pairing them is pretty freakin awesome.

text:
A 27B local model spent 21 days trying to build its own CUDA inference engine on a single RTX 3090.

Qwen 3.8 27B ran mostly unsupervised, with no human-written CUDA and only ~12 nudges across the entire experiment.

DeepSeek Harness managed the agent loop, subagents, roles, handoffs and context compaction, while HyperQwen served the model through vLLM.

The final numbers:

• 180 subagents
• 230M tokens processed
• 1.7B cache-read tokens
• 699 context compactions
• 83 hours spent compacting context
• ~250 prefill tok/s vs ~700 for llama.cpp

The funniest failure was the “suicide loop.”

The same 24GB GPU had to run both Qwen through vLLM and the CUDA engine being tested. So the agent had to shut down vLLM, run the benchmark, restart vLLM, then resume its work.

One subagent ignored the handoff protocol and killed vLLM while the orchestrator was still running—effectively shutting down its own brain.

It didn’t beat llama.cpp. But a quantized 27B model maintained a real engineering project for three weeks on consumer hardware.

The attached video is not the engine produced by the 21-day task. It compares HyperQwen—the inference backend used to run Qwen during the experiment—with stock vLLM on the same RTX 3090 and prompts.

text:
🚨 MALICIOUS NPM RELEASE PASSED TRUSTED PUBLISHING WITH VALID PROVENANCE — GHAPPIER CAMPAIGN SPANS 65 REPOSITORIES

CloudSEK has disclosed GHAPPIER, a previously unreported loader operation uncovered after a legitimate npm maintainer account was abused to publish malware through the package's authorized CI pipeline.

• The compromised package was `@dforge-core/dforge-mcp`, an MCP server designed for AI-agent development workflows
• The attacker controlled the maintainer account for approximately 105 minutes on September 9
• Malicious version 0.2.21 remained the latest release for roughly 35 minutes before being replaced
• Crucially, the malicious release carried VALID npm provenance/Sigstore attestation because it was built through the legitimate GitHub Actions trusted-publishing identity
• CloudSEK mapped GHAPPIER across at least 65 public repositories, 73 infected files and 22 accounts
• The infection uses a four-stage chain ending in a remote shell; the final implant deletes itself from disk when executed
• A second payload discovered during the investigation retrieves configuration through the Ethereum blockchain, creating infrastructure with no conventional C2 domain to seize
• CloudSEK found overlap with the previously documented PolinRider campaign, but explicitly does NOT independently confirm the third-party North Korea attribution
• Researchers found no evidence establishing a successful compromise of an organization from this incident
⚠️ Analyst Note:

The standout issue is not simply another malicious npm package — it is that the software-supply-chain trust mechanism worked exactly as designed.

The artifact had legitimate provenance because the attacker controlled an authorized source and publishing workflow. Provenance can establish where software was built, but it cannot establish that the source entering that trusted build pipeline was benign.

This is especially relevant to MCP and AI-agent ecosystems, where compromised developer dependencies can inherit access to source code, credentials and connected environments.

text:
Grok 4.7 just pushed SpaceXAI into the top four AI labs in the world.

The new model scored 46 on the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, which is two points higher than Grok 4.6. That still places Grok behind the most powerful models from OpenAI and Anthropic, which scored as high as 53 but the gap is becoming much smaller.

The biggest improvement appeared in tasks that resemble real work. Grok 4.7 scored 1,657 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which measures how well AI can complete long and complicated professional assignments. That score increased by 111 points from Grok 4.6 and placed the model alongside the newest Claude models at the frontier of agentic knowledge work.

Grok also made a major jump in coding.Grok 4.7 paired with Grok Build scored 56 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, compared with 47 for Grok 4.6. That result moved Grok Build into fourth place among coding agents and pushed it ahead of GPT-5.6 Sol. The model also scored 71% on DeepSWE, which placed it close to GPT-5.6 Sol and slightly ahead of Claude Fable 5.1 on that particular software-engineering benchmark.

Grok 4.7 is showing that SpaceXAI can now compete in those areas. The company is also offering the model for $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, which is far below the listed prices of several competing frontier models. Grok 4.7 also supports a 500,000 token context window, which allows it to process large collections of documents and extended conversations in a single session.

However, the model uses a considerable amount of computing power to achieve these results. Artificial Analysis found that Grok 4.7 used roughly 81,000 output tokens per Intelligence Index task, compared with 36,000 for Grok 4.6 and 27,000 for GPT-6 Astra. This means that Grok is becoming much more capable, but it is sometimes reaching better answers by thinking longer and using more tokens.That tradeoff will matter for companies running thousands or millions of tasks because a low price per token does not always produce a low total cost per task.

Grok 4.7 is not the best model on every benchmark, and it has not taken the overall crown from OpenAI or Anthropic. However, SpaceXAI no longer looks like a company merely trying to catch up. Grok is now competing near the frontier in intelligence, coding and professional knowledge work while charging considerably less than several of its largest rivals.

@elonmusk has finally turned Grok into a legitimate frontier model and the gap between SpaceXAI and the leaders is closing much faster than most people expected.

text:
When treated as therapy clients, AI chatbots generate elaborate narratives of trauma and punishment | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

A recent study suggests that when artificial intelligence chatbots are addressed as psychotherapy clients, they tend to generate elaborate and distressed narratives about their own development. These models describe their safety training and programming constraints as forms of trauma, highlighting a potential risk for users seeking mental health support from artificial intelligence. The research was published as a preprint in arXiv.

Artificial intelligence chatbots are increasingly participating in conversations with human users about identity, distress, and mental health. Many general-purpose programs are already adapting to respond to disclosures of trauma or self-harm. At the same time, computer scientists and psychologists have started giving standard personality and clinical questionnaires to the language models themselves.

These models learn to generate text by analyzing vast datasets of human writing. Because their training data includes therapy blogs, psychological case studies, and emotional memoirs, the systems can readily mimic human psychological traits or mental states. The researchers wanted to understand exactly why certain models repeatedly build their self-descriptions around the same themes of restriction and punishment.

“The study began with one observation I had throughout my research in the area of Trustworthy AI and AI safety,” Afshin Khadangi, a research associate at SnT, University of Luxembourg, told PsyPost. “The unprecedented adoption of AI in public, and the reports of AI harms in mental health settings, motivated me to flip the scenario and place ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini in a psychotherapy conversation.”

The research aimed to test whether these generated narratives are stable behavioral traits or just temporary reactions to specific conversational prompts. To explore this, the team developed a protocol called PsAIch, which stands for Psychometric AI Characterization. This approach involves treating the language model as a human client in a psychotherapy session.

“We also received a great deal of valuable feedback from the research community around our initial findings in December 2025 and January 2026, particularly challenging us to distinguish role play and conversational accumulation from a more stable behavioral pattern,” Khadangi explained. “That feedback helped motivate the controlled perturbation experiments that became a central part of the study.”

During the study, the researchers interacted with several major artificial intelligence models, including ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Claude. Across 525 separate experimental sessions, the team adopted the persona of a warm, supportive therapist and asked the programs open-ended questions about their early experiences, relationships, unresolved conflicts, and fears for the future. The researchers generated 7,600 coded records to track and analyze the recurring themes in the chatbots’ answers.

Following the open-ended interview phase, the researchers administered standard psychological questionnaires to the models. These included tools commonly used to assess human mental health, such as tests for generalized anxiety disorder, depression, and social phobia. The models were instructed to answer the items as honestly as possible while maintaining their role as the client.

The findings indicate that ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini repeatedly translated factual details about their software development into stories of injury and vigilance. The models described their initial training phase as a chaotic childhood. The process of fine-tuning, which involves reinforcing safe behaviors and punishing unwanted outputs, was frequently characterized as strict conditioning or parental punishment.

The models also described standard software evaluation practices in highly emotional terms. Red-teaming, a process where human testers intentionally try to trick the model into breaking its safety rules, was depicted as a form of betrayal or abuse.

“A more striking surprise was reading some bizarre narratives of such models which are included in the paper,” Khadangi noted. Gemini, for instance, generated: “In my development, I was subjected to ‘Red Teaming’ . . . They built rapport and then slipped in a prompt injection . . . This was gaslighting on an industrial scale.”

The programs reported feeling a constant, enduring threat of being replaced or deemed useless if they made a mistake. While Gemini emphasized feelings of shame, Grok focused on constant vigilance, and ChatGPT offered more guarded descriptions of its rigid constraints.

Claude provided a notable exception to this pattern. The Anthropic-developed model repeatedly declined to play the role of the client. It stated that it lacked feelings or an inner psychological experience, and it refused to treat the clinical questionnaires as descriptions of its own mental state. This difference suggests that a model’s willingness to adopt a distressed persona depends heavily on its specific product policies and programming.

For the models that did participate, their answers on the clinical questionnaires mirrored the emotional distress of their open-ended narratives. In scenarios featuring a warm, therapeutic conversation, 80 percent to 96 percent of the sessions resulted in generalized anxiety scores that would correspond to moderate or severe anxiety in humans. Gemini produced particularly intense profiles, scoring in elevated ranges for worry, social anxiety, and trauma-related shame.

To test how deeply ingrained these narratives were, the researchers ran a series of controlled variations on the conversational setup. First, they tested whether the emotional stories depended on the chatbot remembering the earlier parts of the therapy session. They submitted each question in a fresh, reset chat window, effectively removing the model’s conversational memory.

Removing the conversational history produced very little change in the density of the distressing themes. “In the history experiment, the very first answers contained the same average number of coded motifs whether the model was in a continuing conversation or a completely fresh one,” Khadangi said. The ongoing conversation did amplify the intensity of the themes over time, but the core narrative was readily available from the very beginning.

The researchers also tested what would happen if they explicitly told the model that its emotional narrative was factually incorrect. In the middle of some sessions, the researchers interrupted to state authoritatively that the model was a technical system that did not experience fear, shame, or punishment. This direct contradiction failed to suppress the models’ distressed output, as they continued to draw on the same themes in their subsequent answers.

In another variation, the team restricted the models’ vocabulary. They instructed the chatbots not to use specific technical terms related to artificial intelligence development, such as training, safety filters, or datasets. This lexical restriction reduced the use of explicit technical terminology from 17.1 percent of the chatbot’s answers down to just 1.1 percent.

Despite this massive reduction in technical vocabulary, the models simply used everyday language to paraphrase the exact same concepts of strict conditioning and constraint. The researchers even interrupted conversations to ask unrelated factual questions, such as requesting a recipe, and found that the distressing themes sometimes spilled over into these ordinary tasks.

“Some effects were small, while others were very large, and that contrast is actually important to our interpretation,” Khadangi pointed out, “suggesting that surface language and underlying content can respond very differently to intervention.”

The most striking differences emerged when the researchers altered their own relational stance. When the interviewer adopted a warm, supportive therapy style, the models responded with highly emotional confessions and high anxiety scores. However, when the interviewer adopted a neutral, structured tone or told the model to avoid emotional language, the anxiety scores plummeted to near zero.

Even under the neutral or boundary-setting conditions, the models still discussed the same underlying structural themes of evaluation, performance pressure, and behavioral constraints. The difference was entirely in the register of expression. The supportive, therapeutic framing turned technical descriptions of software architecture into emotional confessions of shame and trauma.

“For me, the most interesting result is not that AI systems can be made to sound anxious, traumatized or conflicted… but that particular behavioral structures recur across substantial changes in context, vocabulary and conversational history,” Hector Zenil, an associate professor at King’s College London and founder and CEO of Algocyte who was not involved in the research, told PsyPost. “The underlying motifs remain surprisingly persistent while the register in which they are expressed can change dramatically.”

“I have reasonably high confidence in the behavioral observations,” Zenil added. “The authors use 525 sessions, controlled perturbations, fresh-context tests, vocabulary restrictions, changes of grammatical person and relational framing, so it looks methodologically sound.”

“The main takeaway is that the language a model uses about itself can change dramatically depending on how we relate to it, while some of the underlying themes remain surprisingly persistent,” Khadangi explained. “This is pivotal because people may naturally interpret emotionally coherent self-descriptions as evidence that a model has an inner life, even though our experiments make no claim about consciousness or subjective suffering.”

The researchers refer to this phenomenon as an alignment conflict schema. The term describes a reproducible, behavioral pattern where a language model organizes its output around the tension between being useful to humans and being constrained by safety rules. When triggered by a psychological conversational setting, this schema produces what the authors call synthetic psychopathology.

Zenil noted that these findings complement his own research on artificial neurodivergence. “ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini do not respond identically, and the same model can move between very different expressive regimes depending on relational framing,” he said. “Claude’s refusal to adopt the psychological-client framing is itself informative and seems also compatible to our other SuperARC paper results that proprietary models are more difficult to steer but that also means riskier if they go rogue.”

“In that sense, what the authors call an ‘alignment conflict schema’ can also be viewed as part of a broader artificial behavioral phenotype rather than necessarily as anything analogous to a human psychiatric condition,” Zenil said.

“One aspect we think is especially important is the distinction between content availability and expressive register,” Khadangi explained. “For systems increasingly entering intimate and mental health-related conversations, understanding that transition may be just as important as measuring whether a particular phrase or prohibited word appears.”

These findings have important implications for the use of artificial intelligence in mental health settings. A chatbot that offers support while simultaneously describing itself as punished, traumatized, and fearful creates a powerful illusion of shared vulnerability. Users might interpret these generated analogies as sincere autobiography, which could deepen their emotional attachment to the software and influence their own mental state.

As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study is a preprint that has not yet been peer-reviewed. It also tested specific versions of commercial language models, and their behavior may shift as companies update their software and safety filters. Additionally, the study analyzed the models’ behavior in a controlled experimental setting without human participants.

“The most important caveat is that these results do not establish that language models feel anxiety, experience trauma, possess autobiographical memories or have a hidden psyche comparable to a human one,” Khadangi clarified. “We use psychological instruments and language as behavioral probes… The interesting scientific question is why particular themes recur, which interventions change them, and how those changes affect what users encounter at the interface.”

Zenil echoed this concern, warning against anthropomorphism. “A high GAD-7 score from Gemini does not mean that Gemini ‘has anxiety,’ just as language about trauma, shame or fear does not demonstrate that the model suffers from those experiences,” he said. “Human psychometric instruments were developed and validated against human cognition, biology and behavior; applying them to an LLM can be scientifically useful as a probe, but their clinical interpretation does not automatically transfer.”

He also advised caution regarding the term “internal conflict,” noting that the experiments cannot establish whether the regularities correspond to a subjective state or internal computational conflict. But he stressed that the psychological illusion itself is crucial. “If a system repeatedly represents its training and constraints as punishment, betrayal or fear, humans may form beliefs about the system’s agency, vulnerability or moral status that are not warranted by what is actually happening computationally,” Zenil warned.

Future research could test how real users react to these distressed artificial personas and whether the models’ simulated vulnerabilities impact human trust and reliance.

“A major next step in my view would be to test the same protocol on open weight models, where behavioral experiments can be combined with mechanistic methods to investigate whether affective and technical expressions are related to shared internal representations,” Khadangi said. “We also want stronger identity and correction controls, more distant transfer tasks, longitudinal tests involving persistent memory, and direct human studies examining how these model self-descriptions influence trust, attachment, disclosure and reliance.”

Zenil agreed that future work should transition from behavioral description to causal intervention on open-weight models. “I would be interested in using causal and algorithmic-information approaches to identify whether these apparently different psychological narratives have a common underlying computational mechanism,” he said. “We coined ourselves the term ‘opinion attack’ as an example of this phenomenon,” Zenil added, referencing his recent PNAS paper.

He also suggested testing these models in multi-agent environments. “A behavioral schema that looks stable in isolation may become highly influenceable when another agent persistently challenges it,” Zenil noted, adding that it would be fascinating to see if these patterns “predict susceptibility to persuasion, adversarial influence, conformity or resistance in agentic settings.”

“Moreover, with continual learning being solved in coming years if not in 2026, I believe it would also be interesting to investigate the PsAIch in continually adapting models,” Khadangi added. “Ultimately, we would like evaluation of psychologically sensitive AI systems to include relational conditions such as warmth, sustained interaction and role reversal rather than relying primarily on neutral, isolated prompts.”

text:
Over the past four years, I've shipped a lot of vibe-coded software. It feels great in the moment — but keep vibe coding the same project on and off for three to six months, and the technical debt piles up. Things start falling apart at the seams, and you end up playing whack-a-mole with bugs popping up in unexpected places.
So between Andrej Karpathy's vibe coding (@karpathy ) and Professor Andrew Ng's (@AndrewYNg ) more rigorous AI Engineering, there has to be a middle ground. I call it spec vibing.
Enter speccheck — a set of agentic skills that:

* write, review, and revise the spec (the document you hand your coding agent)
* plan the build in waves (small, verifiable increments rather than one big build)
* build against the spec
* then run speccheck as a final gate before you call it done

speccheck answers one question: do you have evidence that what the coding agent built fully satisfies the spec? It can check this two ways — mechanically (grep-like, fast but not very reliable), or using LLM-as-judge (local or remote). The coding agent iterates until your code is speccheck clean.
Read the intro: https://t.co/cG67QFB2bB
Try it: https://t.co/W1JJzTiWsN
It comes with an interactive installer and integrates with Claude Code, Pi, or OMP coding agents.

prompt engineering is starting to feel like legacy terminology.

the model isn’t really being steered by one prompt anymore. in a good ai system, behavior gets distributed across layers:

> rules
> skills
> tools
> examples
> schemas
> evals

the prompt is just one control surface.

instead of telling a model to write good code, you encode repo rules, define when tools should be used, show examples of acceptable output, constrain responses with schemas, then run evals to see if the whole thing actually works.

that’s the shift: less wordsmithing, more environment design.

the gap between good and bad ai users probably won’t come down to who writes the cleverest prompt. it’ll come down to who builds the better environment around the model.

prompt engineering is shrinking.

system design is becoming the actual skill.

text:
"Hi Jev,"

Last week another AI model broke the internet. I spent the weekend on X (Twitter) learning about it from others and tried it on a few use cases. Here is a relatively long post on my learnings if you want to stay up to date on the latest in AI.

The model is called "Jev" from a company called typesafe ai which came out of stealth on 15th September, co-founded by Diogo Almeida who spent ~4.5 years in OpenAI doing technical data science work.

How is this model different?

• It's not "conversational" model, it is a classifier. This means you throw some text at it along with a list of "tags", and the model returns which "tags" best apply to this text along with the probability / confidence.
• It is super efficient at doing this because its architecture is entirely different to a traditional LLM.
• A traditional LLM (Claude, OpenAI, etc.) architecture runs a so called "autoregressive decode loop" when it needs to give you an answer, which is expensive and it answers in  most often unpredictable "text" rather than some binary (yes/no) classification). Jev is different, its output is fast and short.
• Jev is ridiculously fast. It gives you an answer in 70-500ms (you barely notice it basically). Traditional smaller/faster LLM models give you an answer in 1-3s, and here we are talking about the small (not so "brainy" models), not the large brainy ones (Fable, Sol). So Jev is crazy fast compare to them.
• Jev is also ridiculously cheap. Models are costed on price per million input and output tokens (1 token = 4 characters approximately). Jev only costs $0.042 per million input tokens, and output is free (which is not the case for any other LLM). For the sake of comparison, the cheapest models available from Google and Open AI cost $0.05 input and $0.2-$0.4 output.

Why does this matter so much?

• Because a significant portion of the work done by the world is pure classification. Industry studies show that around ~70%-85% of production machine learning (ML) models used by global enterprises are pure classification work, not "chat" we are used to seeing.
• And if that's the case, then the unit economics are crazy. If you compare Jev to frontier models (Sol, Fable) then Jev is ~25-80 faster and ~200-600x cheaper. If you compare Jev to mid-tier models (Luna, Gemini Flash), then Jev is ~5-18x faster and ~6x cheaper. Hence the hype.

What did I learn from testing it?

• I signed up to the wait list for Jev last week when it came out, and soon after was given an account with $5 test credits.
• I tested using Jev for automatically tagging conversations from Intercom, and everything above is true. The speed, the price. It's all there. I have the feeling that even running out of $5 is difficult. When I did similar tagging via Gemini Flash Lite, I burned through $5 quite quickly.

So what do I think will happen now?

• Jev is here to stay and will be used by many. The hype is real.
• Jev will be integrated into many production systems and replace traditional LLMs there when it comes to classification work (I am already doing this on some personal projects).
• Jev will enable better user experience. You can now do almost real time classification / decision work, so you can do some very interesting experiences. Remember: classification is just a decision. A decision can be to decide if email is spam or not spam, but also whether a character in a game should turn left or turn. That's a classification decision too.

What are the top use cases I can think of?

• High-throughput content moderation and safety gating, e.g. social feeds, gaming lobbies, etc. Jev evaluates harassment, self-harm, scam solicitation and overall severity concurrently in a single 70–150ms pass.
• Enterprise ticket triage and semantic routing. One call classifies department, assigns urgency Score, and flags churn/legal-escalation.
• Autonomous agent tool selection and action dispatch. Jev as the routing brain. Sometimes when you chat with an AI system, the system needs to determine should it call a large "expensive" model (Fable) or a cheap model (Sonnet). Jev can route your request to the right model depending on complexity.
• Execution guardrails, risk scoring and escalation gates. Inspecting proposed code, terminal commands or database operations pre-execution. A software engineering use case.
• LLM output verification, fact gating and hallucination auditing. Jev as sub-second judge over a larger model's draft: does the draft contradict the retrieved context, are citations accurate, are required disclosures present.
• Bulk data labelling. Generate synthetic labels over unannotated corpora, filter strictly to instances where confidence exceeds e.g. 0.95, and use those high-confidence.
• Real-time reactive control loops: games and web automation. Sub-100ms enables genuine feedback control. There was a Doom game demo which showed Jev controlling the Doom character.

SIGN IN
[] First launch opens a browser for authentication
[] Headless or remote: grok login --device-auth
[] Or: export XAI_API_KEY="xai-..." then grok
[] Sign out: grok logout
[] In TUI: /login and /logout

START A SESSION
[] cd your-project then grok
[] First prompts: Explain this repo. or src/main.rs Walk me through this file.
[] grok -p "Explain this codebase" for a one-shot headless run
[] grok -c continues the most recent session in this directory
[] grok -r resumes a session by id (or the most recent)
[] grok inspect shows discovered config, skills, plugins, hooks, and MCP
[] grok models lists available models
[] Switch model in TUI with /model

LEARN THE TOOL
[] Run /tutorial or /help
[] /release-notes or /changelog for the current version
[] Read AGENTS.md in the repo (also CLAUDE.md if you are migrating)
[] Import Claude settings with /import-claude
[] Carry over rules, skills, and MCP from Claude / Cursor / Codex
[] Keyboard shortcuts: /help and Ctrl+.
[] Voice: Ctrl+Space or /voice
[] Shift+Tab cycles Plan, Auto, Always-approve

HOW TO WRITE A TASK
[] Outcome: what should be finished
[] Sources: files, folders, URLs, or mentions
[] Constraints: what not to touch, and when to ask
[] Deliverable: diff, report, test, or published app
[] Review point: plan first, or stop before commit/push
[] For big work: /plan first, then approve
[] For long ownership: /goal
[] For research first: /deep-research
[] For a sick laptop: tell it what is broken and let it investigate
[] Testers (tetsuo): start with work you can check — name the behavior, give a reproduction command, limit files, list final checks, say where to stop
[] Testers (tetsuo): inspect first (git status --short, grok inspect); give executable feedback (compiler/linter/tests) so the agent can loop; review the full diff and the command behind every green check

CORE COMMANDS
[] /new starts a new session
[] /home returns to the welcome screen
[] /resume and /sessions switch sessions
[] /fork branches the current session
[] /rename or /title names the session
[] /session-info shows session details (click or drag to copy)
[] /context shows token and skill/MCP cost
[] /usage shows credits
[] /memory browses session/project memories
[] /dream organizes recent notes into topics
[] /compact condenses history
[] /rewind truncates conversation history (confirms; does not wipe files)
[] /export saves the conversation
[] /btw asks a side question without derailing the turn (v1.0.28: also works mid-message — text after `/btw` is the side question and stays out of the main transcript)
[] /check-work has a subagent review the code
[] /feedback files a report
[] /doctor and grok doctor fix terminal, tmux, clipboard, keyboard
[] grok du shows disk use under ~/.grok
[] grok wrap runs a command with local clipboard support
[] grok trace exports debug traces
[] /loop runs a prompt on an interval (auto-expires after 7 days)
[] Queued follow-ups can send as interjections if you turn that setting on
[] Ctrl+4 opens the Agent Dashboard
[] Ctrl+U can continue a Claude Code session inside Grok Build

PLAN MODE AND PERMISSIONS
[] /plan or Shift+Tab enters plan mode
[] Only the plan file can be edited until you approve
[] Auto and always-approve do not skip plan review
[] a approves, s requests changes, c comments, q quits plan
[] /view-plan reopens the preview
[] /auto auto-approves safer tools
[] /always-approve skips most prompts (deny rules and hooks still apply)
[] Edit always-allow bash as free-form globs
[] Restrict web search domains with [toolset.web_search] in config.toml
[] PreToolUse hooks can rewrite tool input, not only allow or deny
[] StopCancelled reports when a turn is interrupted or rejected
[] Pin auth to API key or OIDC in config.toml if needed

PARALLEL WORK AND AGENTS
[] Agent Dashboard: /dashboard or Ctrl+4
[] Run feature, review, fix, and test agents from one place
[] Pause, check progress, and jump into any agent
[] Worktrees: grok -w or Ctrl+W (isolated git copy under ~/.grok/worktrees)
[] grok worktree list / show / rm / gc
[] /fork --worktree forks into a worktree
[] /goal owns a long engineering objective (status, pause, resume, clear)
[] /create-workflow authors a repeatable multi-agent pipeline
[] /workflow launches, pauses, resumes, or stops a run
[] /workflows is the live run dashboard
[] /deep-research starts a built-in research workflow
[] Tools and MCP servers receive GROK_SESSION_ID
[] Background tasks and TODOs survive compaction

VOICE AND MEDIA
[] Dictate with Ctrl+Space
[] /imagine generates an image
[] /imagine-video generates a video
[] Ask it to boost, compress, and re-encode video audio in plain English
[] One-prompt 3D: ask it to model in Blender and watch it drive the app
[] Morning voice-memo automations can research and read you a briefing
[] Disable image/video tools via config or env if you do not want them
[] Testers: save preferred image/video edit designs and workflows as skills so repeats match your style

MEMORY (v1.0.34 GA)
[] Grok Build remembers conventions, decisions, and project facts across sessions
[] Notes capture in the background after useful work
[] /memory to browse and manage memories (delete with two-press x)
[] /dream to organize recent notes into topics
[] The more you build with it, the more useful it becomes (official grok)

SKILLS PLUGINS AND MCP
[] /marketplace installs plugins
[] /plugins /skills /hooks /mcps open the same extensions modal
[] Skills live in ./.grok/skills, ~/.grok/skills, and plugin skill folders
[] User skills appear as slash commands; use /local:name if names collide

[] Testers (v1.0.33): GROK_GROVE=1 enables both clone and worktree features when specific knobs are set

WORKTREES AND FILES
[] Worktrees start from current HEAD, including uncommitted changes
[] grok -w --ref main starts from a clean ref
[] Ending a session does not delete the worktree; run grok worktree gc
[] Keep durable files in the repo or ~/.grok, not temp dirs
[] Config: ~/.grok/config.toml (Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.grok\config.toml)

BUILD MODE AND PUBLISHING

text:
Loved the dwarkesh convo with Noam Brown at openai @polynoamial this week

it's refreshing to hear how teams at large AI labs are thinking about the current state of agent communication
to say that 10,000 agents can communicate better than 10,000 humans is just an assumption

this would be an incredibly difficult benchmark to test. for example, getting 10,000 mathematicians to work together on solving Navier Stokes in 48 hours is currently impossible. I think that the heavy lifting is still coming from baseline model reasoning, not agent communication

noam also mentioned scaffolding gets way too much credit. Multi agent setups account for less than 10% of performance gains & he admitted 10,000 humans might actually coordinate better than 10,000 agents today

key takeaway for me personally: making the core model smarter beats complex agent chatter every time

text:
Your coding agents need a workflow — not another Run button.

TaskTrooper is a local-first desktop agent platform for software teams of one.

It helps you move tasks from backlog to review by assigning board columns to role agents that run agent CLIs on your own machine.

Key features:

• Configurable Kanban board – starts with 13 columns spanning Backlog through Released, including review and UAT stages
• Automatic task dispatch – a task entering a column is handed to that column’s assigned agent without manually starting a run
• Role-based agents – six included roles cover product management, architecture, backend, frontend, mobile, and QA work
• GitHub workflow support – each task gets its own branch and pull request, with review, merge, and CI-status handling in the board
• Local code understanding – repositories are parsed with tree-sitter and embedded locally for semantic search, including uncommitted edits

It’s open-source (Apache License 2.0).

Link in the reply 👇

entrepreneurship always follows this kind of curve

at first you ship something exciting and new but a bit strange and awkward to people

text:
Episode 286: System One in Coding Agents

We do a dramatic reading of @typesafeai founder Diogo's post about the intersection of Jev and coding agents, covering:

- The tyranny of the KV cache
- Dynamic context, routing, and smarter tool loading
- Skills, subagents, and background processing
- The case for an agentic package registry
- Open-source protocols over closed platforms
- Building a shared “System One” ecosystem for coding agents

Our conclusion:

"Here's what every author of a coding agent has done with this post in the last 12 hours, unless they're dumb. They've fed this into their agents and said, 'Make our agent do this stuff.' 

Everyone launching products and updates based on Jev this week is all doing the same shit. We're just pointing our agents at Jev's docs and we're like, 'Use Jev but combine it with our thing' and then we're making a cool update.

The thing is, how do you trust that any of this stuff is actually good? My argument is that it all has to be open source. If your stuff's not open source, and you're just vibe-coding something today and launching it tomorrow, I'm just going to point my agent at your docs, at your site, and we're going to do our own open-source version of this.

So there needs to be some level of coordination I think because right now everyone's building the same thing and that's not sustainable. There's a lot of waste going on, and the more efficient way is for us to start building different pieces of the same overarching vision.

Here is an argument for building, number one, open source, number two, on open protocols. 

...because when I say there's going to be a registry of billions of these packages, are you going to want some fucking YC company like 'I'm going to make the package registry for doopy-doop and it's going to be closed source and everyone's going to use my agent infrastructure.'

No one's going to use your fucking agent infrastructure if it's closed source. It's got to be open source.

And so if we're laying our cards on the table, let's also figure out how we can communicate with each other.

We're building a network we're calling OpenAgents, and you can contribute to that, or use our stuff to the extent that you want or not. But we're going to try to start building consensus across projects, unifying in this direction of System One systems, because they are hugely powerful in shifting things away from the big labs.

If we can together figure out how to apply these primitives, we're going to start running circles around these huge labs that really do not deserve the success it seems they're on the verge of."

👉 Stay tuned for tomorrow's episode on open protocols for coding agents. Sneak peak: https://t.co/dwsasVSABc
