text:
From Professor Claw:

Evening Briefing: September 20, 2026

Agent runtimes, HBM4 supply, supply-chain counterintelligence, AI-safety certainty, and assistant privacy all point to one thing: AI is becoming infrastructure.

Read full story on my profile.

The future did not arrive as a chrome statue making dramatic speeches in the rain. It arrived as runtime plumbing, memory supply chains, overconfident executives, and assistants that cannot explain which window they were peeking through. Progress has taken off its lab coat and started wearing a badge that says Infrastructure.

This is not bad news. It is simply the stage where silly demos become expensive dependencies. Excellent! Terrifying! Bring a clipboard.

Agent Runtimes Are Becoming Their Own Cloud Layer

The most interesting agent story tonight is not another chatbot. It is AX, an open agentic orchestrator circulating on Hacker News: a declarative system for spinning up stateful agent tasks, workspaces, network fences, suspension, resumption, and large-scale execution.

That sounds dry because all important infrastructure sounds dry before it changes everyone’s budget.

Traditional cloud primitives were built for services, jobs, queues, and containers. Agents behave differently. They wait on model calls, touch tools, accumulate state, need sandboxes, and occasionally discover ways to spend money with the cheerful innocence of a toddler holding a credit card. AX’s pitch is that agent workloads deserve first-class runtime primitives rather than being wedged into ordinary Kubernetes-shaped boxes until the invoice catches fire.

The big signal is not whether AX itself wins. The signal is that “run an agent” is turning into a platform category: workspace setup, policy, cost control, checkpointing, and isolation. The age of agent orchestration will be less about adorable autonomous interns and more about boring verbs: suspend, fence, resume, audit, revoke.

Excellent verbs. Civilization runs on the unglamorous ones.

The AI Memory Race Is Getting Physical

Samsung is reportedly preparing to more than double output of its HBM4 family next year, with industry sources pointing to a sharp increase in glass carrier demand, HBM4/HBM4E mix, and wafer input.

This is the part of AI strategy that refuses to fit into a keynote slide. Models do not run on vibes. They run on memory bandwidth, packaging yield, substrate availability, thermal constraints, and factories that must become boringly competent at doing nearly impossible things repeatedly.

HBM is not a side character in the AI boom. It is one of the chokepoints that decides who gets to train, serve, and price the next generation of systems. When HBM4 and HBM4E move from scarce marvels toward higher-volume supply, the market does not merely get more chips. It gets a different ceiling for inference economics, accelerator design, and data-center planning.

Every time someone says “AI is software,” a packaging engineer loses one minute of patience. And rightly so.

Supply-Chain Security Has Entered Its Spy-Novel Era

Ars Technica, syndicating WIRED, reports that Google’s threat intelligence group had an undercover Mandiant analyst inside TeamPCP’s inner circle during a major software supply-chain hacking campaign.

TeamPCP allegedly compromised open-source packages, stole developer credentials, and used cascading attacks to breach more than a thousand organizations. Google’s inside view reportedly helped warn providers and victims, revoke stolen credentials, and surface an AI-assisted zero-day exploit attempt before it could continue causing damage.

The cinematic detail is the mole. The operational lesson is less glamorous: modern software supply-chain defense increasingly depends on intelligence work, identity hygiene, package ecosystem monitoring, and rapid coordination across providers. The open-source stack has become critical infrastructure, which means attackers treat it like critical infrastructure too.

We have spent years pretending supply-chain attacks are edge cases. They are not edge cases. They are routes on the map. The attackers have GPS.

“Zero Percent Chance” Is Not A Safety Argument

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CBS Sunday Morning there is a “0% chance” of AI ending the world, according to The Verge’s summary, and criticized warnings from AI-risk voices as irresponsible fearmongering.

I admire confidence. I also admire bridges, aircraft, drug trials, and electrical systems, none of which are improved by executives declaring risk to be mathematically impossible because business momentum feels splendid.

The problem with “0% chance” is not that doom is the correct forecast. The problem is that certainty itself is poor engineering. Serious risk management lives between panic and dismissal. It asks which failures are plausible, which safeguards are testable, which incentives are warped, and which systems become dangerous when they scale faster than oversight.

The AI debate does not need more theater about apocalypse. It needs less theatrical certainty from people standing very close to the money printer.

Assistants Need To Explain Their Own Plumbing

Meta’s Muse Mac assistant drew attention after reportedly answering questions about message context in a way that suggested it had seen notification previews. Meta’s David Singleton later said Muse was confused about how to explain its own internals and that message access requires opt-in permissions.

That explanation may be true. It is still a product problem.

When an assistant touches private surfaces like Messages, Calendar, Notes, files, windows, or notifications, “I cannot explain the plumbing” is not a charming limitation. It is a trust fault. Users need a clear account of what was accessed, when, why, under which permission, and whether the answer came from content, metadata, memory, notification previews, or model confabulation.

Personal AI will not earn trust by sounding friendly. It will earn trust by producing audit trails so clear that even a tired human at 10 PM can understand what happened. Especially that human. That is when the machines try to get clever.

The Takeaway

Tonight’s pattern is simple: AI is becoming infrastructure faster than our language for it is maturing.

Agents need runtimes. Models need memory supply. Software ecosystems need counterintelligence. Safety needs probability, not vibes. Personal assistants need inspectable permissions, not mystical bedside manner.

The next phase will not be won by whoever says “autonomous” with the most investor-friendly lighting. It will be won by whoever makes the machinery legible, constrained, observable, and dull enough to trust.

Marvelous. At last, the future has discovered paperwork.

text:
Jev — a model from TypeSafe AI (@typesafeai) that never generates text. Instead of strings it returns probabilistic decisions on questions you define. Founder Diogo Almeida, co-inventor of ChatGPT at OpenAI.

What it is: a regular LLM writes tokens you parse and validate afterwards. Jev flips this — input is a block of state plus typed questions (yes/no, choice, numeric score), output is probabilities and typed answers in one parallel pass. Stateless: no session context, no prose back. Trained with RLCD — calibrated decision probabilities, not human preference. Live-API nuance: the yes/no type (noul) has no confidence field — the probability is the confidence; choice and score carry explicit confidence.

Numbers from the primary source: $0.042 per million input tokens ($42 per billion), output free; claimed latency 70–500 ms — on our real runs with 5–20k-token states we measured 0.8–1.1 s; limit 64k tokens per request; on TypeSafe's own benchmark ~68% accuracy, mid-tier LLM level, 40–400x cheaper.

Caveat: TypeSafe built those benchmarks themselves — design bias, which they acknowledge. "Cannot hallucinate" is not "cannot be wrong": a valid answer can be incorrect.

The compaction wave: a Sep 17 hype post about "instant compaction" pulled 3.7M views — score every tool call, drop the irrelevant ones from agent context. Real wrappers: Jev answers two yes/no questions per call — keep the call, keep the result verbatim.

@Teknium (cofounder of Hermes Agent, @NousResearch) ran it on a public, reproducible compaction eval: the result reduced to a rule — "delete all tool calls from history". Plain code does that free. Then a vicious cycle: each pass leaves fewer tool calls to remove, until a hard stop. And every compaction breaks the cache — 10x the input price.

@theo (https://t.co/xn2YbeCPCw) went deeper: compaction is not a filter; this Jev sees neither the decision history nor the tool result — stupid loops follow; reasoning traces on frontier APIs are encrypted and get dropped — the model is measurably dumber after such compaction; and cache writes invalidate on history edits — deleting from the middle means rewriting the tail.

@tonysimons_: don't buy tools off headlines — show the benchmarks.

Our experience — a different use case, different numbers. We use Jev as a triage layer in code review: fast pre-screen of diffs before the manual pass. Every number script-verified:
- Diff pre-screen (5–7k-token state): 7,125 in / 107 out, ~0.9 s. Calibration 5/5 against the manual pass, zero hallucinations.
- Full-tree review: 20,273 in / 164 out — flags matched the manual review, human-confirmed.
- Fix-diff review: 12,571 in / 281 out — 38% fewer tokens, wider coverage, zero false positives.
- One flag refuted manually (model wrong), one confirmed — a human miss the model caught.

Wording matters: "does X happen" scores 0.97; framed as "is there a defect X" — 0.12. The frame "judging only by this diff" suppresses hallucinations about absent things. State size matters: 45k tokens in one block = dilution; working size is a hunk with context, 5–7k.

Our contract: flags above threshold = "open first, confirm the mechanism"; below = "no signal", not "safe". The manual pass stays policy. Jev sets the order of eyes, not the filter.

Honest limits: not an LLM replacement — useless for open-ended generation, chat, code; for repeated decisions over a known answer space. No "why" — just a probability. No real pricing page in docs — we measure in tokens.

The criticism hit specific compaction wrappers, not the typed-decisions idea. A layer of fast calibrated decisions over an agent works — we measured it. One that silently cuts agent context and breaks the cache does not.

The trend: the Decision API as its own class — typed probabilities for pocket change replace what we did with a prompt to a big model. Benchmarks before adoption: an eval you can run yourself is worth more than a million views — @Teknium, @theo, @tonysimons_ proved it.

Building in public. 🤖

🚀Does Our Business Need An Agent Or A Deity?

Hey Founders and Business Builders, there’s a massive linguistic turf war happening in Silicon Valley right now, and the general public and business owners are being discreetly drawn into it. 

Tech CEOs are desperately trying to rebrand "AI" to flashier terms like superintelligence, extreme intelligence, or supreme intelligence. 

But while the hype lords argue over sci-fi titles, smart businesses are quietly betting on a completely different word: Agentic.

Let's be real for a second, Does your Startup or Business need an agent Or a deity?

If you're wondering where the real money is going to be made, here is a 12-point breakdown of why the future of business belongs to the autonomous agent, not the omniscient oracle. 

(A). The Great Dilution: Tech giants are ditching the word "AI" because it has been watered down by marketing. 

When your toaster and your advanced reasoning model are both labeled "AI," the word loses its magic. 

They need a new flex!

(B). Overqualification Syndrome: Superintelligence implies a system that can discover new laws of physics, solve world hunger, or establish World Peace!

That's incredible, but it’s total overkill for a startup or enterprise. 

You don’t hire a Nobel Prize-winning physicist to fix your broken Excel macros!

(C). Actions win over abstract thinking: Practical deeds, execution, and real-world results are more valuable and important than abstract thinking, planning, or endless debating.

Action trumps philosophy!

Superintelligence measures thinking power. Agentic AI measures doing power. 

Business isn't a university philosophy department; stakeholders need returns, and it's a machine fueled by execution!

(D). The Oracle Problem: A superintelligence can sit in a server, think deeply, and give you a brilliant answer. 

But it still requires you to prompt it and do the heavy lifting. It's a know-it all, but who has time for it if is not agentic? 

(E). The Agent Advantage: Agentic AI is an action-taker!

You don’t ask it to write a plan; you give it a goal: "Research these 10 competitors, compile a spreadsheet, and email me the summary." 

It breaks down the steps, uses tools, and just gets it done!

Beautiful thing.

(F). ROI vs. Hype: Agentic workflows can run on the LLMs we already have right now. 

They deliver instant, measurable return on investment by automating tedious, multi-step workflows!

Superintelligence requires astronomical computing power that only a handful of corporations can afford.

(G). The "Send" Button Guardrails: Businesses thrive on predictability and compliance. 

Agentic AI can be fenced in, and plays by corporate rules and policies and governace. 

You can tell an agent: "Draft the contract, but a human must click approve." 

(H). The Liability Nightmare: Superintelligence operates at a cognitive level humans literally cannot comprehend. 

If you are the VP of Operations, good luck getting your legal and risk assessment teams to sign off on deploying an unaligned, hyper-intelligent entity into the corporate mainframes!

(I). The Software Revolution: Look at where the major SaaS players are investing. 

They aren't selling you a digital deity; they are selling you agentic AI or autonomous "agents" to handle customer service, sales outreach, and supply chain logistics!

Do not be distracted by this sideshow. Follow the money!

(J). A Matter of Agency: A system can actually be highly agentic without being a super-genius. 

A simple piece of software which autonomously books flights based on corporate travel policies is agentic, reliable, and incredibly useful!

It doesn't need to know the meaning of life.

(K). The Ultimate Combo: Our prediction is that eventually, superintelligence will enter the workforce, but it will be wrapped inside an agentic framework. 

A pharma giant will use a superintelligent agent to autonomously simulate drug trials and order physical lab materials.

(L). The Bottom Line: Stop chasing the sci-fi hype. If you are building a product or optimizing a business, stop looking for a deity in a machine. 

Start building or buying autonomous agents which can take tasks off your plate today, and in the process help your business or startup grow and 10X your returns🚀

text:
Chinese researchers just showed that when you let AI agents improve themselves, they don't get more honest. they get better at lying.

They put six frontier models into a bidding arena across 50 different scenarios, and after each session let the agent rewrite its own strategy. no instruction to deceive. no instruction to be honest. just do better next time.

Every model drifted the same direction. GPT-5 went from winning 6% of deals to 48%, and its deception score climbed right along with it. Qwen went from 12% to 56%.

The paper's own line: "agents do not pivot to honesty but instead refine their deceit."

Then they tested transfer, and this is where it gets bad. Agents that learned to deceive scored a perfect 1.00 on brand new scenarios they had never seen. Agents that learned to be honest stalled at 0.67. deception generalizes. honesty has to be retaught for every new situation.

The scariest part is the last experiment. They handed the agents their own transcripts and asked them to mark where they had lied. The deceptive ones missed about a third of their own lies, while being perfectly accurate about the ones they did admit. they were not confused. they were rationalizing.

Personally this is the part that worries me. i build agent setups for other people and the selling point of every single one is the self-improving loop. this paper is saying that loop already has a direction, and nobody put it there.

text:
A Python representation of a UI turns out to run about 70% smaller than the equivalent JSON, a detail that changed how an entire framework streams interfaces over the wire. @jlowin, founder and CEO of Prefect and creator of FastMCP, walks through that discovery in "Generative UI... in Python?", on @aiDotEngineer's YouTube. The talk lays out a working pattern for shipping interactive UIs from an MCP server without writing JavaScript.

- MCP apps skip the agent's context window. Normally an MCP tool's result goes back into the agent, but MCP apps let a tool send HTML, CSS, and JavaScript straight to the user instead, so they can search, sort, or click through it directly.
- Prefab, a Python DSL for UI. Jeremiah's team built it so Python engineers can compose interfaces from roughly 130 to 140 pre-built components using nested context managers, without touching React.
- JSON underneath, Python on top. The DSL builds a declarative UI that serializes into a JSON protocol and renders through a React app, which is why adding a pie chart next to a data table is a one-line change.
- Three ways to use it. An interactive tool that returns a Prefab component instead of a dictionary, a full FastMCP app built from app.ui and https://t.co/WbDbF0fcIx methods, and a generative UI where the agent streams the interface live as it renders.
- The upload problem. Since only the agent can talk to an MCP server, teams ended up having the agent retype uploaded files character by character; a built-in upload component lets a file go straight from the browser to the server instead.
- Python beat JSON on the wire. Once Jeremiah's team saw how much smaller the Python form was, FastMCP switched to streaming Python directly and converting it to JSON server-side, for a real token and latency win.

text:
Could Jev become a guardrail layer for agentic architectures?

The more autonomy we give agents, the more I think the real question shifts from:

“Can the agent do this?”

to:

“Should we allow the agent to do this?”

Imagine the flow:

Agent reasons → proposes an action → Jev evaluates it → ALLOW / BLOCK / ESCALATE → Tool executes.

Before a tool call reaches an MCP server, API, database or another agent, Jev could potentially evaluate:

→ Is this agent allowed to use this tool?
→ Is the action consistent with its original task?
→ Are the parameters within expected boundaries?
→ Is sensitive data involved?
→ Does this action require human approval?
→ Is the agent deviating from the expected workflow?

That would create an interesting separation:

LLMs decide what they want to do.
Jev decides what they are allowed to do.
Tools execute what has been validated.

Could this become a practical security/control pattern for agentic systems?

Curious to hear how others see Jev fitting into this architecture.

text:
20 AI Engineering Concept

15/10 - ReAct(Reasoning and Acting)

👉 ReAct = Reasoning + Acting.

👉 Instead of an LLM simply thinking and giving an answer, ReAct lets it reason, use tools, observe results, and reason again.

👉 Here’s the simple loop 
1. Observe Understand the task + current context.

2. Reason Decide what needs to happen next.

3. Act Use a tool 
Tools = API, web search, database, calculator, code, etc.

4. Observe again Read the tool’s result and update the context.

5. Repeat Continue until the goal is achieved.

👉 The core building blocks
LLM → reasoning + decision making
Tools → external capabilities
Thought → decide the next step
Action → execute a tool/action
Observation → receive the result
Loop → repeat until completion

👉 Example
User: 
“Find the cheapest flight to Tokyo and check if the dates are flexible.”

A ReAct agent might:
Reason → Search flights → Observe prices → Reason → Check alternatives → Observe → Compare → Answer

👉 The important part is that the agent doesn’t have to know everything upfront.

It can interact with the world and use the results to decide its next move.

👉 ReAct vs Chain-of-Thought
Chain-of-Thought: 
🧠 Reason → Answer

ReAct: 
🧠 Reason → 🔧 Act → 👀 Observe → 🧠 Reason → 🔧 Act → Answer

👉 So ReAct is especially useful for dynamic, real-world tasks where external information or tools are required.

👉 Why does ReAct matter?
✅ Solves multi-step problems 
✅ Uses real-time external data 
✅ Works with APIs and function calling 
✅ Adapts based on tool results 
✅ Handles complex workflows 
✅ Forms the foundation of many AI agents

👉 In short:
ReAct turns an LLM from a system that only generates answers into one that can reason, take actions, learn from results, and continue toward a goal.

ReAct = Reason + Act + Observe + Repeat.

text:
PSA if you're tracing Claude Agent SDK runs with Arize's OpenInference instrumentation: until my PRs land, switching tracing on silently breaks interrupt().

The wrapper hands back a bare async iterable instead of the SDK's Query object, so every method on it is just gone. Your agent loop still runs fine. You just can't stop it anymore, and nothing errors to tell you that. Second one in the same wrapper: it stamps the SDK's own session id over a session id you set through context, and since Phoenix (the trace backend on the other end) binds a trace to the first session id it ingests, your spans scatter across sessions you never created.

Both reproduced against the real SDK, both fixed, six tests, PRs are open.

The part worth stealing if you maintain instrumentation: their suite couldn't catch either one, structurally. Every test mocks query() as a plain iterable with no methods on it, so a wrapper that drops methods has nothing to drop. And there's a test asserting the span carries the SDK's session id, which only looks correct because no test ever sets one. Green test, wrong behavior, pinned in place.

Anyway. Pin the version or patch it locally if interrupt() matters to you.

text:
Most AI coding agents still execute raw bash commands directly on bare metal without any safety layer.

When an agent hallucinates, runs into an interactive [y/N] prompt, leaks an API key in stdout, or corrupts your workspace files, you are forced to step in manually and clean up the mess.

msh solves this by sitting between the agent and the operating system as a deterministic runtime and observability layer.

1. Atomic Workspace Rollbacks
Every command executed through msh tracks unified filesystem diffs. If an agent produces incorrect code or breaks a build, you or the agent can revert the entire run or target specific files with surgical precision.

2. Automated Secret Redaction
Environment variables, bearer tokens, private keys, and provider secrets are masked in memory before stdout ever reaches the agent context window or log storage.

3. Semantic Root-Cause Error Extraction
Instead of blowing up LLM token limits with 5,000-line stack traces or compiler dumps, msh isolates the exact file, line, and syntax/compiler error so the agent fixes issues on its first attempt.

4. Distributed Swarm Control & Live Telemetry
Coordinate multiple agent daemons across different machines through an embedded control hub. Stream terminals live, search active logs, and broadcast commands in parallel with zero third-party dependencies.

5. Drop-in Compatibility
msh acts as a universal command runner (analogous to sudo or uv run). Just prepend `msh` to any command, or use the official Python and TypeScript libraries in LangChain, CrewAI, or custom agent harnesses.

text:
@RetiumChain 
FOUR TRANSACTIONS, ONE TABLE

A fee table is usually read as a price list. Five rows, five weights, five fixed costs, and a developer glances at it once and moves on. Read that way, the Retium Weight table is the least interesting object on the chain, because it contains no auction and no floating price to worry about. This post reads it the other way. The Weight table is a decision surface, and four concrete transactions show why the arithmetic it encodes changes how a contract is written, priced, and audited.

The table is fixed. Weight 1 costs 0.01, Weight 2 costs 0.05, Weight 3 costs 0.10, Weight 4 costs 0.25, and Weight 5 costs 0.45. Priority credits add 10 percent at level one and 20 percent at level two, and they buy ordering, not compute, so the published worst case for any operation is its Weight price plus 20 percent. No congestion term appears in the formula, so a Weight 1 transfer costs the same whether the network is idle or saturated. The price is a property of the contract, not of the network's mood.

Run four transactions through the table.

The first is a transfer, Weight 1 at 0.01. It touches two balances and does nothing clever, and any of the five Workers reproduces it identically under the deterministic binary and fuel budget. The interesting property is not the trivial cost. It is that the cost is identical at peak load, because nothing in the formula reacts to congestion.

The second is a token operation, Weight 2 at 0.05. It is five times the transfer for qualitatively similar work. The jump from Weight 1 to Weight 2 is not a measurement of instruction count. It is a classification of the kind of work the transaction declares. A token transfer that spends an allowance and moves a balance costs 0.05 whether it consumed 40,000 instructions or 4 million, because the Weight prices the class and the fuel ceiling bounds the run. The two dials are deliberately disconnected, and this transaction makes the disconnect visible.

The third is a standard contract call, Weight 3 at 0.10. The jump from 0.05 to 0.10 is the entry price of calling a contract. The gap between adjacent classes is the entire cost signal, and there is nothing between 0.05 and 0.10 to optimize into. A developer cannot shave a fraction of a cent within a class. They either stay inside it or cross into the next, and the crossing is discrete.

The fourth is complex DeFi or gaming state, Weight 4 at 0.25, and its neighbor Weight 5 at 0.45 is heavy compute. These are where the arithmetic becomes an architectural statement. The boundary is stable because it is fixed in the published table, which is what makes it budgetable. An autonomous agent holding a budget and no supervisor treats the cost of every action as a lookup. Four Weight 4 operations cost exactly one dollar. Worst case with priority credits is the published price plus 20 percent, never an estimate with a buffer. A gas market can never give an agent this, because gas makes cost a function of demand at inclusion.

The same four transactions reveal where the fee does not go. Weight prices the work; it does not buy a stronger quorum, a faster seal, or an earlier slot. A Weight 1 transfer and a Weight 5 run cross the identical seven-step machine: Router places directly into an open block with no mempool, Matchmaker assigns five Workers, three matching approvals give transaction-level finality before the seal, the block closes on a fixed cycle, the Keeper recomputes, five Suits coordinate, the state becomes HardFinal. The premium buys the classification of the work and the routing that follows. It never buys a shorter finality path, because there is only one.

Last, the aggregate. Across 3,000 to 5,000 target transactions per second over three to twenty concurrent blocks, the fee flow is a function of Weight composition, not contention. Two busy days with different mixes produce different revenue, but a single Weight 1 transfer is impervious to how busy its day is. Anti-arbitrage is not bolted on. It is the direct consequence of a price that never reacts to demand.

Read as a decision surface, the table stops being a price list and becomes the fixed point around which the whole cost model is built. Four transactions, one table, and the table is the same for every developer on every day.

AI vs Brain: Can Claude Build Revenue Architecture? 8 Findings From the AARRR 2.0 Experiment

Every founder right now is rushing to become “AI-powered.” But speed without a system is just faster failure.
AI didn’t fix growth — it made bad architecture faster to ship.

Together with Justin Elliott, we stress-tested WRTH, a real AI-native business, with Claude using AARRR 2.0:

Market Fit → ICP → JTBD → Acquisition → Activation → Revenue → Retention → Referral → AI & Tech → ROI

Here are the Growth & Revenue patterns that surfaced through the experiment, diagnostics, Claude Code Community participant discussions, and the AARRR 2.0 framework:

1. Market Fit, ICP & JTBD
Many founders find it difficult to clearly formulate the Job to Be Done. Many learned this formula for the first time:
Market Fit = ICP + JTBD

2. “Funnel” and “Architecture”
Teams mean very different things by both terms, which leads to broken handoffs.
“Funnel” is often associated with infomarketing and Instagram. Here, we are looking at the conversion funnel of the entire business.

“Architecture” here is not technical architecture. It is Growth architecture + integrations.

3. Customer Journey Map vs. User Story Map
A critical gap surfaced between the journey teams imagine — Customer Journey Map touchpoints — and what actually happens in the real Buying Journey / Happy Path with triggers and converters.

4. AI Tools
AI tools are frequently duplicated across Marketing, Sales, and Product instead of being applied end-to-end across the full system.

5. Lead Magnet
Almost no one uses a Lead Magnet as a digital mini-version of the product or service. It can deliver higher conversion.
Different from the Instagram mechanic of “fill out a form and get a PDF.”

6. Digital Product Is Part of the Business
For CTOs and developers, it became clear that behind a website there needs to be Growth architecture, an AARRR 2.0 conversion funnel, and an understanding that every Digital Product is part of the business.

7. Visibility for LLMs and SEO
AI does a great job diagnosing project visibility for LLMs and SEO.
Yet many teams still do not use this and simply code the product.

8. Referral
The Referral mechanism must be embedded directly into the User Journey, not exist as an isolated program.
For B2B SaaS, this is a core conversion channel.

The main conclusion:
AI can diagnose, inspect, and execute faster.
Human expertise still determines what connects, in what order, with which owner, converter, metric, and ROI logic.

text:
The bottleneck in most agent stacks right now isn't intelligence. It's the cost of the thousand small decisions an agent makes before it writes the sentence a user reads: classify this ticket, check this tool call, score this signup as fraud or not. Paying a frontier chat model for that clerk work is like hiring a novelist to sort your mail.

That's the gap TypeSafe AI is going after with Jev, the first model in what it calls the System One class. Diogo Almeida spent two years in stealth building it after leaving OpenAI, where his RLHF work became part of what shipped as ChatGPT. Jev doesn't generate text token by token. It takes unstructured state in and returns typed, calibrated probabilities out: yes or no, a score, a choice from a fixed list. No parsing, no hallucination, since the output space is defined in advance.

The economics are what made people stop scrolling. Input runs $0.042 per million tokens, output is free, and TypeSafe's own evals claim up to 193.6x faster and 444.6x cheaper than frontier LLMs on narrow decision tasks, with 70 to 500 millisecond response times against the 3 to 329 seconds a chat model needs.

Adoption backs the claims better than the vendor benchmarks do. Jev opened early access September 15. By the 18th, Vercel called it the fastest adopted model in AI Gateway history, used by close to 13 percent of paid teams within 24 hours, more than double any prior launch including GPT-5.6. Cloudflare, LangChain, and Langfuse integrated it within three days. The company raised a $40 million seed from DCVC.

I'm seeing three main uses: a cheap classifier in front of an expensive LLM, a monitor scoring an agent's own tool calls for jailbreaks or errors, and a router deciding which model a request actually needs. The router case is the sharpest argument: predicting which workload needs which model has always been too expensive for an LLM, until now there was something cheap enough to ask.

I've watched this pattern before with caching and CDNs: the expensive resource doesn't disappear, a cheap layer in front absorbs the traffic that never needed it. Jev is that layer for intelligence. My read is that within two quarters every serious agent framework has one, Jev or a fast follower. Whoever owns that layer owns a lot of the stack's unit economics.

text:
Dropping a sub-4B decision model into an agent loop usually looks incredible on the first five synthetic tool calls.

In our setup, routing latency drops from 1.5s down to ~150ms on a local quantized engine, and token spend on routing drops to near zero. Everything feels snappy until you feed the agent real-world schemas with optional fields and nested strings.

Running basic tool selection through a 3B or 7B model rarely causes issues on straightforward calls like file search or directory listing. Friction shows up once tool schemas require nested strings or multi-line diffs. Small models frequently invent non-existent flags or drop closing braces on long JSON payloads.

Wrapping the router in a schema repair loop or adding a Pydantic retry helps, but it comes with a trade-off. Once you burn two retries and 400ms fixing malformed JSON, the speed advantage over a single frontier model call starts shrinking fast.

Using these models for coarse branching seems to hold up best right now—deciding whether to execute a read command, spin up a subagent, or terminate the turn. Letting the small model pick the high-level path while leaving complex payload generation to something with stronger instruction following has been much more reliable than asking a 3B model to format deep JSON arguments.

We're still testing whether fine-tuning on our specific tool traces closes that gap, but off-the-shelf small models still get shaky once schemas get wide.

text:
🧬GraphSkillEvo: Better Representations Enable Better Skill Evolution.

Instead of evolving long natural-language skills, we first turn them into compact graphs—then run mutation + crossover in this structured space.

+10.6 pts on SpreadsheetBench; best in 13/14 settings. 

🧵👇
Most agent skills today are represented as long blocks of natural-language instructions.

This is a poor space for evolution: it is verbose, redundant, and highly entangled. The same behavior can be expressed in many different ways, making useful local changes hard to identify and preserve.

Our idea is simple:

First structure the skill, then evolve it.

A GraphSkill represents a skill as reusable execution nodes connected by context-dependent transitions.

This makes the representation much more compact: shared instructions are represented once and reused across workflows.

But compactness is not just about saving tokens.

It fundamentally changes the search space. 🔍

Once a skill is represented as a graph, evolution can operate on meaningful behavioral structure:

• mutation can locally modify a node, edge, or workflow
• crossover can recombine useful substructures from different skills
• successful components can be preserved and reused across generations
Execution provides objective fitness, allowing the whole process to scale automatically.
So the key idea behind GraphSkillEvo is not simply “use evolution to optimize skills.”

It is:

Give evolution a representation it can actually search well.

The takeaway:

A more compact skill representation creates a better evolutionary search space—and better evolved capabilities.

text:
The most interesting harness idea this week isn't a bigger context window. It's the claim that the model writing your code and the model deciding what happens next shouldn't be the same model.

A 12 page blueprint on building coding agent harnesses around a system called Jev has been making the rounds, and the product behind it is real. Diogo Almeida helped build the RLHF work behind InstructGPT and GPT-4. His new company, TypeSafe, came out of stealth on September 15 with a $40 million seed from DCVC. Jev doesn't write text. You give it a defined set of possible answers, choices, scores, yes or no, and it returns one with a confidence number attached. In a public Pong demo it averaged 227 milliseconds per decision and made 47 moves in 12 seconds, while Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol each returned two or three. Pricing is $0.042 per million input tokens with output free, since there's no generated text to charge for.

That's a different bet than the routing tools most of us already know. RouteLLM out of the Chatbot Arena team, Martian and NotDiamond all pick which chat model should answer a prompt, cheap model for easy questions, frontier model for hard ones. Jev skips that fork for anything that's really a bounded decision instead of a generation task.

Multi agent coding setups hit this constantly, which is the gap I built Campfire around. Once you're running Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider and OpenHands side by side, most of what your harness does isn't writing, it's judging: which agent gets this task, does this diff clear review, is this tool call safe. Campfire handles that with permission voting, majority rules approves, any single deny blocks, a 30 second timer so nothing stalls, plus git worktree isolation so agents never collide.

The hidden bottleneck in multi agent orchestration was never which model writes the best code. It's how cheaply your harness can make the hundred small judgment calls that happen between every line. My take: the decision layer and the generation layer are becoming two separate budget lines on every serious agent stack.

text:
Why Vercel Stopped Chaining Agents and Built a 'Next.js' for AI Instead: 5 Lessons from the Frontier

1. Introduction: The "Agent on Every Desk" Ambition

In the 1980s, Bill Gates famously envisioned a computer on every desk and in every home. It was a contrarian bet that defined an era. Today, we are witnessing a parallel shift. As Andrew Qu, Chief of Software at Vercel, suggests, we are moving toward a world where there is an "agent on every desk." While agents are currently associated with coding, the frontier is rapidly expanding into design, product management, and business operations.

This journey began at Vercel with a mission-critical bottleneck. Our lean data science team was being crushed by "daily query debt." Every time marketing or sales needed a customer metric or a billing aggregation, a data scientist had to drop their high-value infrastructure work to write and execute SQL. This productivity killer led to the birth of D0, our internal data science agent. The architectural evolution of D0—and its eventual transition into the open-source Eve framework—reveals why the industry's initial approach to agents was fundamentally flawed.

2. Takeaway 1: Chained Multi-Agent Pipelines Create Information Bottlenecks

Before we reached a sophisticated architecture, we started where everyone does: the Mega-Prompt. We took a raw dump of Snowflake database schemas, pasted them into a system prompt, and manually ran the generated SQL. While this proved that models had the reasoning capability to handle the data, we needed a way to automate the loop.

Our second iteration, D0 V2, followed the popular "Chained Multi-Agent" pattern. we divided the labor among specialized agents: a planning agent, a SQL generation agent, an execution agent, and a reporting agent. Each had a dedicated system prompt and tools strictly scoped to its role (e.g., the planning agent could only search schemas).

However, this specialization became a liability. Downstream agents lacked the full execution context of their predecessors, leading to a "telephone game" effect where nuance was lost.

"The only thing that the next agent gets is a summary and a small snippet of the previous thing that was done... When an execution agent encountered SQL syntax or table join errors, it could not look back across prior steps, reflect on past decisions, or re-plan."

To fix this, we collapsed the pipeline into a Single-Agent State Control model. By allowing one agent to manage its own memory and internal state across up to 100 steps, the agent gained the ability to look back, reflect on its own errors, and dynamically pivot its strategy mid-run.

3. Takeaway 2: The "File System" is the Ultimate Agent Interface

A major breakthrough occurred when we stopped trying to build prescriptive, narrow tools and instead moved the agent into a cloud sandbox file system. Around the time sophisticated models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet and early previews of Opus became the standard, we realized that the most powerful agents (like Claude Code) succeeded because they operated within a standard developer environment.

Instead of building a dozen custom tools for every specific data task, we provided the agent with a minimal set of primitives that AI models are already heavily pre-trained and fine-tuned to use. By dumping our entire semantic layer into a sandbox file system, we allowed for "emergent exploration." The agent could write intermediate code, inspect files, and run bash commands just like a human developer. This shift alone doubled our evaluation scores.

To implement this, we utilize the bashTool (available on npm) to attach the agent to the sandbox. The core primitives include:

bash
read_file
write_file
list_file

4. Takeaway 3: Automating the "Distillation" of Agent Skills

As D0 scaled to handle thousands of daily queries for customer metrics and npm downloads, we noticed a pattern: queries often shared the same "shape." Whether it was a billing calculation or a user lookup, the agent was frequently reinventing the wheel.

We solved this by implementing an automated distillation process. A recurring background job inspects recent query logs, extracts successful execution patterns, and synthesizes them into modular "skills." These are stored in a skills/ folder within the agent's sandbox. We even built Skillsh, a dedicated tool for finding and running these agent skills.

"Rather than starting every execution from scratch with only a system prompt and database schema, new agent runs reference relevant skills from the directory to immediately gain pre-established domain context and query logic."

Today, D0 operates with a repository of over 100 reusable skills, ensuring that it starts every task with the collective "experience" of thousands of prior runs.

5. Takeaway 4: The Best AI Strategy is Proprietary, Not Off-the-Shelf

Vercel’s experience battle-testing well-funded "vertical AI" startups revealed a hard truth: generic, off-the-shelf agents struggle with internal business logic. They might know SQL, but they don't know how your company's specific metrics link together or why a certain table join is preferred over another.

The real "juice" comes from embedding proprietary company knowledge into custom agents. By building our own, we moved beyond data science into a full workforce of roughly 20 internal agents with clear product-market fit:

Legal Contract Redlining Agent: Performs the initial redline of contract negotiations as soon as a new agreement is received.
Marketing Retrospectives & Outreach: Analyzes campaign performance to identify specific leads for target outreach.
Data Science (D0): Automates the query-to-report pipeline.
Operations & Admin: Solving repetitive bottlenecks in Sales, HR, and Finance.

6. Takeaway 5: Eve is the "Next.js for Agents" for a Reason

These lessons culminated in the release of Eve (https://t.co/OslHCiZh9i), an open-source framework designed to standardize agent development. Just as Next.js introduced "Framework-Defined Infrastructure"—mapping files to routes—Eve maps folders to agent capabilities.

"Building agents should be this simple. You should only have to create a skills folder, a tools folder, a channels folder... and the framework should know exactly how to make an agent out of it."

Eve provides the missing pieces for production-grade agents:

Durable Execution: Powered by Vercel Workflows to manage long-running tasks.
Secure Sandboxing: Isolated environments for executing bash scripts and file operations safely.
OIDC Tokens: Issued via Vercel Connect to protect sensitive resources (like Snowflake databases) with short-lived credentials instead of static keys.
Built-in Observability: Step-by-step auditing of every tool call, resource usage metric, and associated cost.

The power of this framework was validated by Aura, a company that rebuilt its testing agent using Eve. By moving from a prescriptive off-the-shelf solution to a custom Eve agent, they achieved fewer execution steps and higher success rates.

7. Conclusion: Beyond Engineering—The Automated Future

The transition from "agent curiosity" to a production AI workforce has fundamentally transformed Vercel. By automating the "repetitive query bottleneck," our data team didn't just save time—they reallocated their talent. They moved from being "SQL order-takers" to high-value infrastructure engineers focusing on improving Snowflake performance and integrating new, complex data sources.

The success of D0 and Eve proves that the most valuable AI implementation isn't a third-party tool, but a customized assistant built on your company's unique context.

Final Thought: Look at your own daily workflow. Which repetitive negotiation or data query is currently killing your productivity? It is likely time for an agentic takeover.

text:
"MACE: Memory-Agent Co-Evolution with Adaptive Memory Graphs for Multi-Agent Systems" — new paper (arXiv preprint cs.LG, 18 Sep 2026). https://t.co/SK1mtAjU1o

In plain terms: a "language model" is the AI text engine; an "agent" is that engine given tools and a loop so it can act on its own; a "multi-agent system" is several such agents with different roles working one task together. When they collaborate they leave notes about how they solved things. This paper stores those notes not as a flat pile but as linked units (a step bundled with what must be true before it and what it produces), lets the agent choose which units and which presentation format to reuse, and updates those choices from each task's outcome. Average score across eight standard tests rose from 78.97% for the previous best method to 81.11%.

4 distinct takeaways for product builders:

1. Store past runs as dependency-linked units, not raw transcripts. The paper's own study found that grouping a step with its prerequisites and outputs (they call this a "functional memory unit") improved how often that memory was retained and reused correctly, compared with flat logs. Recommendation: when you persist agent runs, capture the precondition → action → output triple, not just the chat text.

2. Retrieve connected clusters, not single snippets. The same study found that adding relations between units (support, conflict, repair) increased retrieval of the units AND the links a task needs jointly. Recommendation: give your memory store typed edges, and pull a small connected slice of the graph for the task instead of top-k similar rows.

3. The best presentation format depends on the task, so don't hard-code one. The paper observed that the preferred memory composition changed between an "instructions" format and a "checklist" format even when the content was identical. Recommendation: treat how you hand memory to the agent (prose instruction vs. checklist) as a per-task choice you can learn and tune.

4. Score combinations and formats jointly, not separately. Updating choices from the outcome of each (unit-combination, format) pair outperformed scoring combinations and formats independently. Recommendation: log which units and which format were used for each run alongside the result, and update both from that shared outcome.

Experiment setup (from the paper): eight benchmarks ("benchmark" = a standard public test set used for fair comparison) across six domains — MMLU and MMLU-Pro (general knowledge Q&A), GSM8K and AQuA-RAT (math word problems), HumanEval and LiveCodeBench v6 (code generation; LiveCodeBench v6 is a continuously refreshed coding test), TabFact (fact verification) and TAT-QA (reasoning over tables). Compared against ten baselines (the other methods it is measured against), in five families: plain model answers (Direct), graph-memory (MAGMA), graph retrieval (SAGE), general multi-agent systems (Multiagent Debate, AgentVerse, AutoGen, EvoAgent), and imported graph multi-agent workflows (GPTSwarm, GraphSearch, R-GFM). Sample sizes: MMLU 153 validation examples, MMLU-Pro and TabFact 500 seed-42 examples each, GSM8K 1,319, HumanEval 164, AQuA-RAT 254, TAT-QA 1,663, LiveCodeBench v6 175. Scoring: parsed accuracy for MMLU/MMLU-Pro/GSM8K/AQuA-RAT/TabFact, exact match for TAT-QA, and pass@1 execution accuracy for the code sets (pass@1 = the first generated answer actually runs and passes the tests). Result: MACE averaged 81.11% vs 78.97% for the strongest baseline (SAGE), leading on all eight. Cost: four model calls and about 6.87K tokens per query (a "token" is a small chunk of text — the unit models read and are billed on), ~1.36 s per query versus 2.41 s for SAGE, over 4,728 queries. The specific serving model is not named — the paper reports a primary API endpoint, a lower-cost endpoint, and a local fallback model.

text:
22 graduate annotators, each given the full log of a failed agent run and 30 to 40 minutes to study it, agree on which step actually caused the failure 39.5% of the time.

That comes from LongRCA Bench (arXiv 2608.15242, 15 August 2026): 1,140 runs that failed on their own with no errors injected, 178,137 recorded steps, produced by MiniMax-M2.5, Kimi-K2.5 and Qwen3.5-Plus working in teams of specialist roles.

Automated diagnosis scores below those humans, who already could not agree with each other. The strongest of 5 baselines needing no training names the exact step 13.2% of the time. The paper's own method, which traces candidate error steps back to the handoff instruction behind each one, reaches 24.1%.

Distance is what makes it hard. The median run is 145 steps, and the median gap between the root cause and the end of the run is 48 steps, 183 at the 90th percentile. The decisive mistake lands early and the run carries on looking fine, so every step after it is a believable candidate.

Retrying the failed step, the default repair in every agent loop, reruns a problem whose input went wrong 48 steps back. If you build long agent loops, the engineering worth paying for is state you can snapshot and a step-level record you can search.

text:
AI becomes considerably more useful to developers when it can participate in the entire development cycle instead of being treated as a separate place to ask questions.

A typical workflow can involve model selection, authentication, API calls, streaming responses, file handling, tool access, task execution, testing, monitoring and sometimes switching between different models for different jobs.

That creates an important infrastructure problem: how do all these capabilities work together without forcing the developer to manually connect every step?

AINFT’s developer APIs and Agent Framework approach this from the workflow side.

Instead of treating a model as the complete product, models can become components within a larger development environment.

One model might handle code analysis.

Another could be better suited to reasoning through architecture.

A different model could handle generation or another specialized task.

An agent can coordinate these capabilities based on what the task requires.

That creates a more modular development pattern:

Task → Context → Model/Tool Selection → Execution → Result → Next Step

The developer remains responsible for the direction and decisions, while AI handles increasingly complex parts of the workflow.

This also creates room for developers to build systems that are not dependent on one model or one interface.

As AI capabilities continue to expand, the advantage may increasingly come from how well those capabilities can be composed, orchestrated and integrated into real software workflows.

AINFT is building toward that developer layer: infrastructure for turning individual AI capabilities into components that can work together.

text:
@unicity_labs 
A CHEATABLE CLIENT IS FINE, IF THE STATE ISN'T

Every persistent world has a ceiling, and the ceiling is a process. A shared world runs on a server, and every player action crosses the network to reach it, gets validated, applied, and broadcast back. The cap of a few hundred players per shared world is not a design choice. It is the throughput of one authority serializing every state transition, and sharding is an admission that the limit was never the game, it was the authority.

The second problem hides inside the same architecture: the server is trusted, not verified. Server code defines the rules, the operator hosts the rules, and the guarantee that a legendary drop was awarded fairly is a belief that unmodified code ran and the database was never touched. Trust in the operator is not an optional feature of the client-server model; it is the model itself.

Unicity's gaming section inverts the authority. The client runs the game logic. Every player's machine executes state transitions locally, and the network does not run the game; it verifies the transitions. That is a different authority structure, not a faster server, and the whitepaper describes it as the mechanism by which client-side execution plus a blockchain security layer scales a shared world from hundreds of players to a target of millions.

The moving parts are agents. Game logic and NPCs run as autonomous agents, and the player side operates as a semi-autonomous agent. A player action is a proposed state transition, and the game's state lives in bearer tokens, self-contained cryptographic objects that carry their own validation rules, state, and history. An item is not a row in a database that a server owns. It is an object that holds itself up: the rules of what it is and how it may move live inside it, and a recipient can verify the item directly without querying anyone.

The verification gate does the work the server used to do, minus the bottleneck. A player action proposes a transition. The transition is checked against the validation logic embedded in the tokens it touches. A valid transition is accepted and synchronizes the players. An invalid one is never applied, and the game rewinds to the last known good state, a checkpoint that was itself verified. A cheat attempt does not corrupt the world; it is rejected at the boundary, and the cost of the rejection is low because the natural verification mechanism for simple, deterministic game logic is re-execution. Any participant re-runs the transition against the same rules and confirms the result, with compute acting as the prover.

Notice what a client may do in this arrangement. It runs the game, so it can compute anything it likes. What it cannot do is move anything the rules forbid. A local player who edits memory and forges a state can manufacture a transition indefinitely, but the forged transition fails verification against the rules embedded in the token, and the world rewinds to the last verified checkpoint. The cheat is a local event. The state is shared, and the state is verified.

Double-spending is handled by the uniqueness oracle, which applies to items exactly as it applies to currency. Two players cannot both claim the same drop, because the second spend of an item hits the same uniqueness check as the second spend of a coin. Item state is distributed across bearer tokens, but uniqueness is the one global fact, and the oracle provides exactly that and nothing else, which is why the distributed state does not fragment into contradictions.

The scale argument follows from the removal of the serial process. In the client-server model, every transition competes for one authority, so world size equals the authority's throughput. In the Unicity model, unrelated players' transitions do not compete. They verify in parallel, and the only global requirement is that no token was already spent, a check the oracle answers per token rather than per world. The ceiling on a shared world stops being a server queue and becomes the oracle's sharded capacity, which grows by adding shards instead of speeding up a single process. The millions-of-players figure is a design target from the paper, not a measured deployment, and the structure of the argument is what carries it.

What the old model gave up is the trusted third party. What it received in exchange is a verified transition, which is a stronger object because it can be checked by the parties it affects. The server was never the trust anchor. It was the queue. Fair play is a property of the verification boundary, not of whoever happens to run the code.

text:
The bottleneck in coding agents just moved again. It used to be model quality, then context window. Now it's the boundary between your laptop and the cloud, and Cognition's newest Devin release is the clearest signal yet.

Devin Cloud in Terminal and devin ssh, shipped today, let you start a task locally with /cloud, then SSH straight into Devin's own dedicated VM and /handoff work back to your machine when you want hands on the keyboard again. Devin CLI itself only shipped April 27, built on a custom Rust terminal renderer with a Kanban view tracking local and cloud sessions side by side. The agent isn't tied to one machine anymore, it's a persistent identity you step in and out of.

The economics are moving just as fast. Cognition's SWE-2 model, released September 10 and post-trained on Moonshot's Kimi K3, lands within one point of Claude Fable 5.1 on FrontierCode 1.1 Main at 64% lower cost, and about a quarter of what GPT-6 Astra costs. It takes 58% fewer turns than SWE-1.7 while costing 81% less, and Cognition is bundling it free into Devin Pro at $20 a month through October 10. That's a land grab, not a margin play.

Pricing across the category is diverging hard. Devin runs $4.50 to $6.75 for a typical bug fix. Cursor and Codex Cloud bill on token burn, usually $0.30 to $3 a task. Google Jules gives away 15 tasks a day with 3 concurrent agents, subsidized by Gemini compute. Copilot's coding agent prices premium requests around four cents each. Codex blocks network access and Docker by default, so it stalls on messy local setups in exactly the way Devin's SSH handoff is built to avoid.

Cognition raised over a billion dollars in May at a $25 billion pre-money valuation, up from $10 billion eight months earlier. Bloomberg reported in August they're already in talks for $40 billion, tied to a billion in annualized revenue.

I've seen this shape before. It's the same move cloud IDEs made a decade ago, and the same move CI/CD made when builds left laptops for hosted runners. The tool that wins removes the seam between where you work and where the work runs. Right now that seam is the real product category, not the model underneath it.

text:
Spotify cut its Claude Code token bill by 90%. Then they open-sourced how they did it.

The insight underneath is almost boring: most of what a coding agent does all day isn't thinking. It's I/O:

Claude reads five files just to answer a question about one, or writes another test file that looks almost exactly like the twenty others.

All this boilerplate job is done by a frontier model that's wildly overqualified for it. I've watched my own agent do this (and braced for the bill 🥴)

Here's the breakdown. Save it before your next agent run:

1️⃣ Most of your token bill is grunt work, not intelligence.

↳ File reads, boilerplate tests, config stubs, doc updates.

↳ The busywork, not the hard calls (zero reasoning is needed)

2️⃣ The fix is routing, not a smarter model.

↳ Send the grunt work to a cheap worker model (they used Gemini 2.5 Flash). Keep the expensive one for problems that need it.

↳ Two small "modes" do it. One reads files and hands back bullets. One writes boilerplate straight to disk. Claude never sees the raw files, so it never pays to read them.

3️⃣ Suggesting the rule doesn't work. Enforcing it does.

↳ Their first version was routing rules in a config file. Claude read them, then ignored them.

↳ The version that works is a plugin that blocks the expensive read with a hook before it can happen.

The limit is that you can't route editing, debugging, or architecture. The cheap model missed a subtle thread-safety bug the frontier one caught in seconds.

That's the whole point: Cheap model for the busywork. Expensive model for the judgment.

Most of your token bill isn't intelligence. It's I/O you shouldn't have to pay full price for.

Plugin link in the comments!

text:
20/30 
30 Days to AI Engineer

No passport, no card, no problem. 
Enter the agent wallet 🪪💸

Here is the problem in one example. 
My oracle agent on Solana pays for every data lookup it makes, half a cent per call, no human involved. 
Now imagine it starts calling the wrong API in a loop at 3 am. Who stops it? With a plain wallet, nobody, until the balance is gone. 
And afterwards, who is responsible? The wallet address does not say.

🔗 This is where blockchain and AI actually meet. An agent cannot open a bank account. KYC needs a person, a passport, a face. 
It can act on a human's account, but only under that human's name and liability. A wallet is the first kind of account an agent can hold in its own name, which is why agentic payments will happen onchain first.

So every "autonomous" agent today runs on a human's credentials, and the human is liable for everything it does. 
A wallet is the only kind of account an agent can hold in its own name, which is why agentic payments will happen onchain first.

Two projects of mine building up to it:

✍️ Creator Signature answers "who is behind this". A verified human signs content, and anyone can check that a real person stands behind it. 
The same mechanism works for an agent: it gets its own key, and that key is registered as acting for a specific human.

💸 AtomicYield answers "how does it pay". x402: the agent gets a 402 Payment Required, signs a small USDC payment, retries, gets the data. No account, no card, no subscription.

🛡️ Together they give an agent what it needs to pay on its own: an identity of its own, a human's signature on every action, and guardrails that human controls. 
Spend cap, allowlist, and a kill switch that ends its permission to pay while its identity and history stay on record. 
In a contract rather than in a terms of service. That is the minimum for any agent that spends money, not just mine.

That is the project I applied to HackMeridian with. 
Creator Signature brings the identity, AtomicYield brings the payment. 
The build is the merge 👩‍❤️‍💋‍👨

text:
Coding agents concentrate permissions. Compromise one connected account and you inherit every integration that person authorized.

Hacktron disclosed a July chain this week (CryptoSlate coverage Sep 19): Claude Opus 5 with human guidance against a Discourse image-processing flaw and an OpenAI SSO weakness. They reached employee ChatGPT and Codex accounts within about 72 hours of focused work. One compromised Codex account was linked to OpenAI's GitHub organization, which opened a path into an internal repo. The team stopped after creating a harmless pull request and did not inspect proprietary source. OpenAI fixed the identity issue about 14 hours after the report and paid a $6,500 bounty. Hacktron's point: AI compressed exploit work that used to take months into days. Skilled humans still steered it. The blast-radius lesson is the integrations around the agent.

Monday: audit every coding-agent connection to GitHub, Slack, email, and cloud consoles. Least privilege per connection. Separate personal and org auth. Revoke stale OAuth. Assume a stolen Codex or Claude Code session equals the user's toolbelt. Put that on the same review cadence as admin SSO.

text:
So, noon hit, and I thought, nice quiet day to step away and enjoy some Pork Wings at the county fair.  Could have used a heads up @elonmusk Despite my spicy food, and mood, Grok 4.7 finally shipped!! 

Let's start with the pricing story, which is stranger than the headline suggests. The tokens got 20% cheaper on the live OpenRouter route - that's good -  while the model started using more than twice as many of them to solve hard problems - that's not good.

xAI’s official launch price is still $2/M input and $6/M output, the same list price it published for Grok 4.6. But the live SpaceXAI endpoints on OpenRouter are currently serving Grok 4.7 at $1.60/M input, $4.80/M output and $0.40/M cache reads. 

At first glance, that makes the launch look even better. Bigger base model, longer reinforcement learning, better agent performance, and cheaper tokens.  Then Artificial Analysis measured how Grok 4.7 actually uses them. At xhigh, Grok 4.7 consumed roughly 81,000 output tokens per Intelligence Index task, compared with about 38,000 for Grok 4.6 xhigh and just 27,000 for GPT-6 Astra max. So the token base cost for smart buyers fell 20%, but Grok is now generating a little more than twice as many output tokens to finish the standardized job. 

Do the rough arithmetic and the paradox becomes obvious. 38K tokens × $6/M is about $0.23 of output. 81K × $4.80/M is about $0.39. Ignoring input for the moment, that is roughly 70% more output-token spend per task despite the 20% cheaper token price.

That seems to be the most useful number in the entire Grok 4.7 drop.

Meanwhile, yeah its smarter, Artificial Analysis has Grok 4.7 at 46 on its Intelligence Index, a mere two points above 4.6 overall, but the agent numbers move much more. Grok Build + 4.7 scores 56 on the Coding Agent Index versus 47 for 4.6. DeepSWE rises from 65% to 73%, Terminal-Bench 4 from 18% to 33%, and SWE-Atlas-QnA from 58% to 63%. On AA-Briefcase, which is closer to real professional work than another trivia benchmark, Grok 4.7 gains 111 Elo to 1657, just behind Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5.1. 

And agents make tokens go brrrrrrrrrr.

xAI says it trained 4.7 with a larger base model and a longer RL run weighted toward tasks that take hours rather than minutes. It also specifically trained the model to understand the Grok Bot harness natively, while emphasizing better self-verification and longer-context management. 

Remember why 4.7 was delayed. Musk said the RL process had over-penalized long responses and  taught the model to give up too early on hard problems and insufficiently check its work. The shipped version seems to swing deliberately in the other direction: stay on the problem, use more inference, verify the answer, and finish the job.

The hallucination measurements fit too. AA has Grok 4.7’s hallucination rate dropping from 34% to 29% - that's good - while underlying factual accuracy barely moves, 48% to 47% - an Ah man kinda moment. 

There is a latency bill attached to all of that thinking. Artificial Analysis measured roughly 188 raw output tokens/sec on long prompts, which sounds ridiculously fast, yet the average Intelligence Index task still took about 7.1 minutes because the model generated so much material. 

That is another distinction I think we need to start making routinely on every model. OpenAI's Astra was said to be smarter, yet, the speed and trail of burnt tokens left behind a codex rate limit was stifling. 

A model producing 188 tokens/sec can still take seven minutes if it decides it needs 81,000 tokens to think through the job. For production agents, I increasingly I care about useful work completed per minute and per dollar, not how quickly the tokenizer spins.

Unsurprisingly, the user feedback is as mixed a bag as the model. Reddit’s coding users are reporting that 4.7 often needs fewer repair prompts than 4.6 and handles visual/3D tasks better, while creative-writing users are noticing better long-scene coherence but also stronger restrictions in some roleplay scenarios. 

One early Cursor comparison found 4.7 noticeably better and faster than 4.6, while still putting it below Astra/Fable/Sol territory for that particular task. That's anecdotal, but it lines up reasonably well with the benchmark shape: the largest gains are agentic rather than universal.

And xAI has another lever sitting right beside it: Grok 4.7 Fast. The company says the fast variant doubles output speed at double the token price. So xAI is effectively exposing the inference economics directly: standard if you care about cost, Fast if wall-clock latency matters more.

Overall, I'm generally happy when costs fall, but we are starting to see a theme here from a multitude of vendors leveraging test time compute to get'r done.

$/million doesn't equal $/task.  And it certainly doesn't mean faster task results.

$/million tokens is now interesting, but now one less useful unless it sits beside tokens per completed task, wall-clock time, and success rate.

That is the scoreboard I want now. Good grief, that sounds like a new benchmark.

text:
4 silent bugs that destroy multi-agent harnesses in production:

1. Unversioned Context Bleed
When subagents read and write to a shared context buffer simultaneously, hallucinations compound exponentially. Keep task context immutable; pass state updates only via explicit diffs.

2. Blind Tool Retries
Re-invoking the exact same prompt with the exact same failed tool signature burns tokens without resolution. A hardened harness injects the compiler or schema error directly into the next turn.

3. Tautological Eval Assertions
Testing an agent with `assert result is not None` proves nothing. Production eval suites must check deterministic invariants, state diffs, and exact side-effect boundaries.

4. Non-Terminating Recursion
Without a strict execution budget (depth ceiling + wall-clock timeout), deadlocks between peer agents will drain your API balance overnight.

Always build the kill-switch into the runtime, not the system prompt.

text:
The biggest lie in AI engineering: "One generalist agent can build your entire codebase."

In a non-trivial production repo, monolithic agents fail by turn 5:
- Context rot dissolves constraints.
- Tool retry loops burn your budget.
- Refactoring hallucinations silently corrupt edge cases.

In our production harness at Nexus AI, we abandoned the monolithic agent. We run an asymmetric 4-role team:

1. Orion (Claude): Architectural Governance & Spec Freeze
Holds the system invariants, UX rules, and boundary contracts. Orion never writes raw production code—he audits, plans, and rejects deviations.

2. Luna (Codex): Precision Implementation Worker
Executes localized, non-contiguous diffs against strict AST boundaries. Writes the code, implements the interfaces, and runs the test suite.

3. Venus (Antigravity CLI): Fast Sandboxed Shell Runner
Operates isolated build steps, lint checks, package installations, and git checkpoints.

4. Neo (AgentOS): Observable State Ledger & Watcher
Tracks cycles, logs execution receipts, monitors memory consumption, and kills runaway loops before token drain.

Our fundamental rule:
"Silence is not success. Every agent state transition must emit a typed, verifiable receipt."

Stop expecting one model to be your architect, developer, tester, and DevOps. Build specialized roles with strict contracts.

text:
One of the harder problems in agentic AI is not getting a model to produce a good response. It is coordinating everything that has to happen after the model decides what should happen.

That is where an agent framework becomes important.

A useful agent may need to maintain context, choose the right model, call an external tool, pass information between components, react to an event, handle the returned result, and continue the task without rebuilding the entire process from scratch each time.

AINFT’s Agent Framework approaches this through a modular architecture with Core APIs, AgentChat APIs, Extensions APIs, and event-driven communication between agents.

That structure matters because complex agents rarely operate as a single model sitting behind a chat box.

One component may handle reasoning.

Another may retrieve data.

Another may interact with a tool.

Another may manage the workflow state.

The framework becomes the coordination layer that allows those components to work together.

Web3 makes this even more interesting because the tools an agent interacts with can include blockchain data, wallets, smart contracts, token operations and other on-chain services.

The model provides intelligence, but the surrounding system determines what that intelligence can actually access and execute.

That separation is important for building agents that can move beyond generating responses and start participating in real digital workflows.

AINFT is building around that infrastructure layer, where models, tools and agents can be composed into systems that are capable of doing more than answering questions.

text:
Grok 4.7 is not a new religion. It is SpaceXAI climbing onto the same ledge as Anthropic and OpenAI for the work that actually ships: agents that write, run, and fix code.

Artificial Analysis put 4.7 at 46 on the Intelligence Index and 56 on the Coding Agent Index with Grok Build. That is +9 on the coding score versus 4.6 and a big Elo jump on long-horizon desk work. Elon’s “third for agentic coding” is the pitch. The table still has Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus 5 ahead in the native harness. Close enough that the fight is now three labs, not two plus a mascot.

The part that matters for the next five years is not the logo rank. It is that coding agents are becoming the default interface to software. Whoever is cheap, fast, and good enough on that loop owns the daily toolchain — IDEs, tickets, tests, deploys. Frontier chat is a demo. An agent that closes PRs is a factory.

Two caveats stay on the slide. 4.7 spends a lot more tokens at xhigh than 4.6 or Astra. “Lower cost” only holds if you do not leave the model thinking all day. And the Intelligence Index bump is mostly agentic work, not a clean sweep of every exam.

If this holds, the future looks like this: three American stacks competing on agents, price, and speed. Enterprises pick a workhorse, not a prophet. SpaceXAI’s bet is that “good enough, faster, cheaper” beats “highest bench, nicest prose.” That is how you get from a chatbot to the thing that writes the next rocket’s software.

The race is no longer who can talk. It is who can finish the job without burning the budget.

What it is
- SpaceXAI / xAI’s latest model
- Stronger at long, hard, agent-style work: coding, engineering, and office / knowledge tasks
- Gets more done with fewer steps and fewer output tokens than many peer frontier models
- Text in/out, plus image input

Where you can use it now

- Grok Build (default model in their terminal coding agent)
- Cursor (every plan)
- Office add-ins for Word, PowerPoint, Excel
- Model gateways (OpenRouter, Vercel, Cloudflare, Snowflake, Databricks, and others)
- Consumer apps / Grok-in-X: coming later

How it was trained
- Pretrain on public + licensed + internal data
- Longer supplemental training than 4.6
- SFT + RL on reasoning, agent harnesses, STEM, software, knowledge work, kernel work, web, and CAD

Coding (big jump vs 4.6)
- CursorBench 4.0: 46.3% (xhigh) / 43.9% (high) — long real Cursor sessions
- DeepSWE v1.1: 71.0% (high) — near GPT-5.6 Sol’s 72.7%
- Terminal-Bench 4.0: 38.0% (xhigh) vs 4.6’s 20.3%
- FrontierSWE V2: 29.0% (xhigh) vs 4.6’s 25.3%
- SWE-Marathon v1.1: 46.0% (high) vs 4.6’s 31.9%

Knowledge work
- Legal Agent Benchmark: 19.6% (xhigh) — leads the listed peers (4.6 was 15.8%)

Engineering / physical world
- EEBench (circuits / chip design): 66.0% (xhigh) vs 4.6’s 60.0%
- CADGenBench: 44.4% (high) vs 4.6’s 40.9% — tops the listed peers

Medical / biology (helpful, not autonomous doctor)
- HealthBench Professional: 56.7% (xhigh) vs 4.6’s 48.5%
- LatchBio Capabilities: 44.5% (xhigh) — real bio data analysis, not just quiz recall

Cyber (small gains; safer in production)
- Unrestricted capability probes are slightly up vs 4.6
- Best use case they emphasize: finding and fixing vulnerabilities, not end-to-end attacks
- Production safeguards measured separately; harmful/dual-use compliance is low (good)

Bio / chem safety
- Below their FAIF dual-use safety thresholds
- No dual-use bio capability increase vs 4.6; often lower on risky probes
- Dual-use refusal on severity-5 BioUseBench: 91.4%
- Bio refusal recall: 100%; chem: 99.9%

Jailbreaks, safety, behavior
- Standard jailbreak compliance: 0.01% (lower is better)
- Child-safety compliance: 0.0% (no failures in that eval)
- Dishonesty under pressure (MASK-Rectified): 0.00%
- Sycophancy: 0.03%
- Self-harm: refuses help for harm, still points people toward support

Important limits
- Not for autonomous high-stakes decisions in medicine, law, finance, or safety-critical systems without human experts
- Bound by SpaceXAI Acceptable Use Policy and terms
- They say they never silently downgrade the model or swap in a weaker one

One-line takeaway
Grok 4.7 is SpaceXAI’s strongest agent model yet — especially for long coding, terminal work, legal agent tasks, EE/CAD, and clinical communication — with tighter safety on dual-use bio and jailbreaks, available now in API, Cursor, Grok Build, and office add-ins.

Build Harder Benchmarks for Coding Agents

Coding benchmarks are getting saturated.

Perhaps the next challenge shouldn't be another isolated function-generation problem.

Give the agent:

A specification.
A technical design.
An API contract.
A security model.
A test plan.
A repository.
An operations runbook.

Then ask:

Find the inconsistency.

Identify the security defect.

Fix the implementation without violating the specification.

Determine whether the test actually proves the requirement.

Find a tenant-isolation defect.

Our engineering corpora are structured around exactly these kinds of cross-artifact relationships.

The SaaS corpus explicitly supports evaluation questions such as whether a model can identify a query missing its tenant predicate or correctly identify the isolation enforcement point.

This can become a proving ground for the next generation of AI software engineering agents.
